name: Humanist Perspective
definition_quote: Humanists, including theorists Abraham Maslow (1908–1970) and Carl Rogers (1902–1987), stressed individual choice and free will.
plain_en: emphasizes free will and personal growth

name: Psychodynamic Perspective
definition_quote: Psychologists using this perspective believe that the unconscious mind—a part of our mind that we do not have conscious control over or access to—controls much of our thought and action.
plain_en: unconscious mind controls much thought and action

name: Biopsychology (or Neuroscience) Perspective
definition_quote: Biopsychologists explain human thought and behavior strictly in terms of biological processes.
plain_en: explains behavior through biological processes

name: Evolutionary (or Darwinian) Perspective
definition_quote: Evolutionary psychologists (also sometimes called sociobiologists) examine human thoughts and actions in terms of natural selection.
plain_en: interprets behavior through natural selection

name: Behavioral Perspective
definition_quote: Behaviorists explain human thought and behavior in terms of conditioning.
plain_en: explains behavior through conditioning

name: Cognitive Perspective
definition_quote: Cognitive psychologists examine human thought and behavior in terms of how we interpret, process, and remember environmental events.
plain_en: studies how people interpret, process, and remember events

name: Social-Cultural (or Sociocultural) Perspective
definition_quote: Social-cultural psychologists look at how our thoughts and behaviors vary among cultures.
plain_en: examines how culture shapes thoughts and behavior

name: Biopsychosocial Perspective
definition_quote: This modern perspective acknowledges that human thinking and behavior results from combinations of biological (“bio”), psychological (“psycho”), and social (“social”) factors.
plain_en: combines biological, psychological, and social factors

name: eclectic
definition_quote: This point of view, sometimes called eclectic, claims that no one perspective has all the answers to the variety of human thought and behavior.
plain_en: combines multiple perspectives rather than one

name: Hindsight bias
definition_quote: People have the tendency upon hearing about research findings (and many other things) to think that they knew it all along; this tendency is called hindsight bias.
plain_en: overestimates what one knew in advance

name: Confirmation bias
definition_quote: Confirmation bias is the tendency to pay more attention to information that supports our preexisting ideas
plain_en: favors information supporting preexisting ideas

name: Overconfidence
definition_quote: overconfidence is the tendency to be, well, overconfident about the things we believe
plain_en: overestimates the accuracy of one's beliefs

name: Applied research
definition_quote: This type of research is known as applied research because it has clear, practical applications.
plain_en: research with clear practical applications

name: Basic research
definition_quote: Basic research explores questions that are of interest to psychologists but are not intended to have immediate, real-world applications.
plain_en: explores questions without immediate practical application

name: Quantitative research
definition_quote: Quantitative research uses numerical measures
plain_en: measures variables with numbers

name: Qualitative research
definition_quote: qualitative research typically uses more complex textual responses and looks for key themes within them.
plain_en: analyzes textual responses for key themes

name: Hypothesis
definition_quote: A hypothesis expresses a relationship between two variables.
plain_en: states a relationship between two variables

name: Variables
definition_quote: Variables, by definition, are things that can vary among the participants in the research.
plain_en: factors that can vary among participants

name: Experimental hypothesis
definition_quote: According to an experimental hypothesis, the dependent variable depends on the independent variable.
plain_en: dependent variable depends on independent variable

name: Independent variable
definition_quote: In this hypothesis, watching television violence is the independent variable since the hypothesis suggests that a change in television viewing will result in a change in behavior.
plain_en: variable the researcher manipulates

name: Dependent variable
definition_quote: In testing a hypothesis, researchers manipulate the independent variable and measure the dependent variable.
plain_en: variable measured as the outcome

name: Theory
definition_quote: A theory aims to explain some phenomenon and allows researchers to generate testable hypotheses with the hope of collecting data that support the theory.
plain_en: explains phenomena and generates testable hypotheses

name: Falsifiable
definition_quote: It is essential the hypotheses be falsifiable; that is, it must be possible to gather data that would controvert the hypothesis.
plain_en: possible to gather data disproving it

name: Operational definitions
definition_quote: When you operationalize a variable, you explain how you will measure it.
plain_en: explains how a variable will be measured

name: Validity
definition_quote: Research is valid when it measures what the researcher set out to measure; it is accurate.
plain_en: measures what it is intended to measure

name: Reliability
definition_quote: Research is reliable when it can be replicated; it is consistent.
plain_en: produces consistent, replicable results

name: Sampling
definition_quote: The individuals on which the research will be conducted are called participants (or subjects), and the process by which participants are selected is called sampling.
plain_en: process of selecting research participants

name: Population
definition_quote: The population includes anyone or anything that could possibly be selected to be in the sample.
plain_en: everyone who could possibly be selected

name: Representative sample
definition_quote: The goal in selecting a sample is that it be representative of a larger population.
plain_en: sample reflecting the larger population

name: Random sampling
definition_quote: The definition of random sampling is that every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
plain_en: every population member has equal selection chance

name: Convenience sampling
definition_quote: Using my own students for the research is an example of convenience sampling, collecting data from a group of people who are easily accessible to you.
plain_en: uses easily accessible participants

name: Stratified sampling
definition_quote: Stratified sampling is a process that allows a researcher to ensure that the sample represents the population on some criteria.
plain_en: ensures sample matches population on criteria

name: Confounding variable
definition_quote: A confounding variable is any difference between the experimental and control conditions, except for the independent variable, that might affect the dependent variable.
plain_en: extraneous difference affecting the dependent variable

name: Random assignment
definition_quote: Random assignment means that each participant has an equal chance of being placed into either group.
plain_en: equal chance of placement into either group

name: Group matching
definition_quote: If one wanted to ensure that the experimental and control groups were equivalent on some criterion (e.g., sex, IQ scores, age), one could use group matching.
plain_en: groups matched on relevant criteria

name: Experimenter bias
definition_quote: Experimenter bias is the unconscious tendency for researchers to treat members of the experimental and control groups differently to increase the chance of confirming the researchers' hypothesis.
plain_en: researcher unconsciously treats groups differently

name: Double-blind study
definition_quote: A double-blind study occurs when neither the participants nor the researcher are able to affect the outcome of the research.
plain_en: neither participants nor researchers know group assignments

name: Single-blind study
definition_quote: A single-blind study occurs when only the participants do not know to which group they have been assigned; this strategy minimizes the effect of demand characteristics as well as certain kinds of response or participant bias.
plain_en: only participants unaware of group assignment

name: Demand characteristics
definition_quote: Demand characteristics are cues about the purpose of the study.
plain_en: cues revealing the study's purpose

name: Experimental group
definition_quote: The experimental group is the one that gets the treatment operationalized in the independent variable.
plain_en: group receiving the treatment

name: Control group
definition_quote: The control group gets none of the independent variable.
plain_en: group receiving no treatment

name: Placebo method
definition_quote: Whenever participants in the experimental group are supposed to ingest a drug, participants in the control group are given an inert but otherwise identical substance.
plain_en: control group receives inactive but identical substance

name: Correlation
definition_quote: A correlation expresses a relationship between two variables without ascribing cause.
plain_en: relationship between two variables, not causation

name: Positive correlation
definition_quote: A positive correlation between two things means that the presence of one thing predicts the presence of the other.
plain_en: one variable's presence predicts the other's

name: Negative correlation
definition_quote: A negative correlation means that the presence of one thing predicts the absence of the other.
plain_en: one variable's presence predicts the other's absence

name: Ex post facto (quasi-experimental) study
definition_quote: If I seek to control all other aspects of the research process, as I would in an experiment, I will have conducted an ex post facto (quasi-experimental) study.
plain_en: quasi-experiment that cannot prove causation

name: Survey method
definition_quote: The survey method, as common sense suggests, involves asking people to fill out surveys.
plain_en: asks people to fill out surveys

name: Likert scales
definition_quote: One common type of item used on surveys are Likert scales, which pose a statement and ask people to express their level of agreement/disagreement with the statement.
plain_en: statement rated by agreement level

name: Directionality problem
definition_quote: The inability to tell which of the variables came first (also known as temporal precedence) is called the directionality problem.
plain_en: cannot tell which variable came first

name: Spurious correlation
definition_quote: In this case, there is no real relationship between the two variables being studied at all, and the correlation is known as a spurious (false) correlation.
plain_en: false correlation caused by third variable

name: Naturalistic observation
definition_quote: Sometimes researchers opt to observe participants in their natural habitats without interacting with them at all.
plain_en: observing participants in natural habitat without interacting

name: Qualitative data
definition_quote: Although many surveys are comprised of items that participants select from a set of choices, they also can include open-ended questions where participants can write in their responses; this type of data are qualitative.
plain_en: open-ended written responses

name: Structured interview
definition_quote: A structured interview is like a survey in that there are fixed number of questions asked in a set order.
plain_en: fixed questions asked in set order

name: Semistructured or unstructured interviews
definition_quote: However, interviews can also be semistructured or unstructured, allowing more opportunity for the interviewer to react to the participants' responses and obtain a richer, albeit less controlled, set of data.
plain_en: flexible interviews allowing follow-up questions

name: Case study method
definition_quote: The case study method is used to get a full, detailed picture of one participant or a small group of participants.
plain_en: detailed picture of one participant

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Science Practice 3—Data Analysis
definition_quote: Specifically, in this section you will learn about what the College Board calls Science Practice 3—Data Analysis: understanding and making inferences based on numerical data.
plain_en: making inferences from numerical data

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Descriptive statistics
definition_quote: Descriptive statistics, as the name suggests, simply describe a set of data.
plain_en: summarizes a set of data

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Mean
definition_quote: The mean is what we usually refer to as the average of all the scores in a distribution.
plain_en: arithmetic average of all scores

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Median
definition_quote: The median is the central score in the distribution.
plain_en: central score in a distribution

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Mode
definition_quote: The mode is the score that appears most frequently.
plain_en: most frequently occurring score

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Positively skewed distribution
definition_quote: When a distribution includes an extreme score (or group of scores) that is very high, as in the car example above, the distribution is said to be positively skewed.
plain_en: extreme high score causes positive skew

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Negatively skewed distribution
definition_quote: When the skew is caused by a particularly low score (or group of scores), the distribution is negatively skewed.
plain_en: extreme low score causes negative skew

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Range
definition_quote: The range is the distance between the highest and lowest scores in a distribution.
plain_en: distance between highest and lowest scores

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Standard deviation
definition_quote: The variance and standard deviation are closely related; standard deviation is simply the square root of the variance.
plain_en: measures how spread out scores are

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: z-scores
definition_quote: These z-scores measure the distance of a score from the mean in units of standard deviation.
plain_en: distance from mean in standard deviation units

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Normal curve
definition_quote: The normal curve is a theoretical bell-shaped curve for which the area under the curve lying between any two z-scores has been predetermined.
plain_en: theoretical bell-shaped curve

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Percentiles
definition_quote: Someone who scores in the 90th percentile on a test has scored better than 90 percent of the people who took the test.
plain_en: percentage scoring below a given score

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Correlation
definition_quote: A correlation measures the relationship between two variables.
plain_en: measures the relationship between two variables

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Positive correlation
definition_quote: If two things are positively correlated, the presence of one thing predicts the presence of the other.
plain_en: presence of one predicts the other

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Negative correlation
definition_quote: In contrast, a negative correlation means that the presence of one thing predicts the absence of the other.
plain_en: presence of one predicts the other's absence

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Correlation coefficient
definition_quote: The strength of a correlation can be computed by a statistic called the correlation coefficient.
plain_en: statistic showing a correlation's strength

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Scatterplot
definition_quote: A scatterplot graphs pairs of values, one on the y-axis and one on the x-axis.
plain_en: graphs pairs of values as points

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Line of best fit
definition_quote: The line of best fit, or regression line, is the line drawn through the scatter plot that minimizes the distance of all the points from the line.
plain_en: line minimizing distances from scatterplot points

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Inferential statistics
definition_quote: Whereas descriptive statistics provide a way to summarize information about the sample studied, the purpose of inferential statistics is to determine whether findings can be applied to the larger population from which the sample was selected.
plain_en: applies sample findings to the population

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Sampling error
definition_quote: The extent to which the sample differs from the population is known as sampling error.
plain_en: extent sample differs from population

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: p-value
definition_quote: The p-value gives the probability that the difference between the groups is due to chance.
plain_en: probability difference is due to chance

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Statistical significance
definition_quote: Scientists have decided that a p-value of 0.05 is the cutoff for statistically significant results.
plain_en: result unlikely due to chance

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Practical significance
definition_quote: In addition to statistical significance, psychologists are interested in practical significance—or how large an effect is.
plain_en: how large an effect is

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Replication
definition_quote: When we replicate a study, we conduct it again using the same methodology in an attempt to see if the results will be the same.
plain_en: repeating a study to verify results

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Meta-analysis
definition_quote: Meta-analysis is a type of research that combines the results of many studies on the same topic in order to approximate an average effect.
plain_en: combines many studies into average effect

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Peer review
definition_quote: Prior to publication, psychology studies undergo peer review, a process by which a paper is read by several others in the field and the author is asked to make revisions in order to ensure high quality publications.
plain_en: experts review papers before publication

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Institutional review board (IRB)
definition_quote: Any type of academic research must first propose the study to the ethics board or institutional review board (IRB) at the institution.
plain_en: committee reviewing research ethics

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Clear scientific purpose
definition_quote: The research must have a clear scientific purpose.
plain_en: research must serve clear scientific aims

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Least amount of suffering feasible
definition_quote: Researchers must design experimental procedures that employ the least amount of suffering feasible.
plain_en: minimize animal suffering

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: No coercion
definition_quote: No coercion—Participation should be voluntary.
plain_en: people choose to participate freely

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Informed consent
definition_quote: Informed consent—Participants must know that they are involved in research and give their consent.
plain_en: participants know and agree to participate

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Confidentiality (or anonymity)
definition_quote: Confidentiality (or anonymity)—Participants’ privacy must be protected.
plain_en: protects participants' privacy

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Risk
definition_quote: Risk—Participants cannot be placed at significant mental or physical risk; they must have protection from harm.
plain_en: avoid significant mental or physical harm

chapter: Chapter 3: Statistics and Ethics in Research
name: Debriefing
definition_quote: Debriefing—After the study, participants should be told the purpose of the study and provided with ways to contact the researchers about the results.
plain_en: explains study purpose afterward

name: Neuroscience or biopsychological perspective
definition_quote: The influence of biology (sometimes called the neuroscience or biopsychological perspective) is growing.
plain_en: studies psychology from a biological viewpoint

name: Genetic predisposition
definition_quote: The term genetic predisposition refers to the increased chance of developing a specific trait or condition due to our genetic code.
plain_en: inherited tendency toward a trait or condition

name: DNA
definition_quote: The genetic material that makes up chromosomes is DNA—deoxyribonucleic acid.
plain_en: chromosome material holding genetic information

name: Genes
definition_quote: Certain segments of DNA control the production of specific proteins that control some human traits. These discrete segments are called genes.
plain_en: DNA segments controlling specific protein production

name: Dominant or recessive genes
definition_quote: Genes can be dominant or recessive. If we inherit two recessive genes for a particular trait, that trait is expressed. In any other combination of genes, the dominant trait is expressed.
plain_en: dominant expressed with one copy; recessive two

name: Identical twins (monozygotic twins)
definition_quote: Since identical twins (called monozygotic twins since they develop from one fertilized egg called a zygote) share all the same genetic material, researchers study them in order to examine the influence of genes on human traits.
plain_en: twins from one fertilized egg sharing all genes

name: Chromosomal abnormality
definition_quote: Occasionally, chromosomes will combine (or fail to) in an unusual way, resulting in a chromosomal abnormality.
plain_en: unusual chromosome combination or number

name: Turner’s syndrome
definition_quote: For example, babies with Turner’s syndrome are born with only a single X chromosome in the spot usually occupied by the 23rd pair.
plain_en: born with only one X chromosome

name: Klinefelter’s syndrome
definition_quote: Babies born with Klinefelter’s syndrome have an extra X chromosome, resulting in an XXY pattern.
plain_en: extra X chromosome producing XXY pattern

name: Down syndrome
definition_quote: Babies with Down syndrome are born with an extra chromosome on the 21st pair.
plain_en: extra chromosome on chromosome pair 21

name: Neuroanatomy
definition_quote: Neuroanatomy refers to the study of the parts and function of neurons.
plain_en: study of neuron parts and functions

name: Neurons
definition_quote: Neurons are individual nerve cells.
plain_en: individual nerve cells

name: Dendrites
definition_quote: Dendrites—rootlike parts of the cell that stretch out from the cell body.
plain_en: rootlike branches extending from cell body

name: Cell body (soma)
definition_quote: Cell body (also called the soma)—contains the nucleus and other parts of the cell needed to sustain its life.
plain_en: neuron's main part containing the nucleus

name: Axon
definition_quote: Axon—wirelike structure ending in the terminal buttons that extends from the cell body.
plain_en: wirelike structure extending from the cell body

name: Myelin sheath
definition_quote: Myelin sheath—a fatty covering around the axon of some neurons that speeds neural impulses.
plain_en: fatty covering around axon, speeds impulses

name: Terminal buttons
definition_quote: Terminal buttons (also called end buttons, terminal branches of axons, and synaptic knobs)—the branched end of the axon that contain neurotransmitters.
plain_en: branched axon ends containing neurotransmitters

name: Synapse
definition_quote: Synapse—the space between the terminal buttons of one neuron and the dendrites of the next neuron.
plain_en: space between terminal buttons and next dendrites

name: Neurotransmitters
definition_quote: Neurotransmitters—chemicals contained in terminal buttons that enable neurons to communicate.
plain_en: chemicals enabling communication between neurons

name: Resting potential
definition_quote: In its resting state (also referred to as resting potential), a neuron has an overall slightly negative charge (–70 mV) because mostly negative ions are within the cell and mostly positive ions are surrounding it.
plain_en: slightly negative neuron charge at rest

name: Threshold
definition_quote: If enough neurotransmitters are received (this level is called the threshold), the cell membrane of neuron B becomes permeable and positive ions rush into the cell, bringing the charge within the cell to approximately +40 mV.
plain_en: stimulation level required to trigger firing

name: Action potential
definition_quote: The change in charge spreads down the length of neuron B. This electric message firing is called an action potential.
plain_en: electric impulse traveling along the neuron

name: All-or-none principle
definition_quote: It’s important to note that a neuron either fires completely or does not fire; this is called the all-or-none principle.
plain_en: neuron either fires completely or not at all

name: Depolarization
definition_quote: This process of neural firing is also called depolarization because the cell fires due to the resting potential of the cell—its negative charge—becoming “depolarized” when positive ions rush into the cell, changing the overall charge from negative to positive.
plain_en: positive ions entering make charge positive

name: Excitatory neurotransmitters
definition_quote: Some neurotransmitters are excitatory, meaning that they excite the next cell into firing.
plain_en: neurotransmitters that excite the next cell

name: Inhibitory neurotransmitters
definition_quote: Other neurotransmitters are inhibitory, meaning that they inhibit the next cell from firing.
plain_en: neurotransmitters that inhibit the next cell

name: Sensory neurons (afferent neurons)
definition_quote: Sensory neurons, or afferent neurons, take information from the senses to the brain.
plain_en: carry sensory information from senses to brain

name: Interneurons (association neurons)
definition_quote: Once information reaches the brain or spinal cord, interneurons (also called association neurons) take the messages and send them elsewhere in the brain or on to efferent neurons.
plain_en: connect sensory and motor neurons within CNS

name: Motor neurons (efferent neurons)
definition_quote: Motor neurons, or efferent neurons, take information from the brain to the rest of the body.
plain_en: carry information from brain to body

name: Organization of the Nervous System
definition_quote: Our nervous system is divided into different categories based on function. The two main divisions are the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system.
plain_en: two divisions: central and peripheral nervous systems

name: Central nervous system (CNS)
definition_quote: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of our brain and spinal cord—all the nerves housed within bone (the skull and vertebrae).
plain_en: brain and spinal cord

name: Spinal cord
definition_quote: The spinal cord is a bundle of nerves that run through the center of the spine.
plain_en: nerve bundle running through center of spine

name: Afferent nerves
definition_quote: Sensory neurons in your toe are activated, and this message is transmitted up a neuron that runs from your toe to the base of your spine (afferent nerves).
plain_en: nerves carrying sensory messages toward CNS

name: Reflex arcs
definition_quote: However, humans have a few reflexes that work differently: reflex arcs. Certain reactions occur the moment sensory impulses reach the spinal cord.
plain_en: involuntary reactions handled by the spinal cord

name: Peripheral nervous system (PNS)
definition_quote: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) consists of all the nerves in your body that are not part of the central nervous system—that is, all the nerves not encased in bone.
plain_en: nerves outside CNS, not encased in bone

name: Somatic nervous system
definition_quote: The somatic nervous system controls our voluntary muscle movements.
plain_en: controls voluntary muscle movements

name: Autonomic nervous system
definition_quote: The autonomic nervous system controls the automatic functions of our body—our heart, lungs, internal organs, glands, and so on.
plain_en: controls automatic functions like heart and organs

name: Fight-or-flight response
definition_quote: These nerves control our responses to stress: the fight-or-flight response that prepares our body to respond to a perceived threat.
plain_en: body prepares to respond to perceived threat

name: Sympathetic nervous system
definition_quote: The sympathetic nervous system mobilizes our body to respond to stress.
plain_en: mobilizes body to respond to stress

name: Parasympathetic nervous system
definition_quote: The parasympathetic nervous system has the opposite job of the sympathetic system. It carries messages to the stress response system that cause many of our body activities to slow down and return the body to homeostasis (its typical level) after a stress response.
plain_en: calms body, returns it to homeostasis

name: Endocrine system
definition_quote: Another part of human biology relevant to psychology is the endocrine system. This is a system of glands that secrete hormones that affect many different biological processes in our bodies.
plain_en: glands secreting hormones affecting body processes

name: Adrenal glands
definition_quote: The adrenal glands produce adrenaline (also known as epinephrine), which signals the rest of the body to prepare for fight or flight.
plain_en: produce adrenaline preparing body for fight or flight

name: Ovaries and testes
definition_quote: Ovaries and testes produce our sex hormones, estrogen for females and testosterone for males.
plain_en: produce sex hormones estrogen and testosterone

name: Ways of Studying the Brain
definition_quote: As mentioned previously, the first challenge of brain research is creating a way of detecting brain function.
plain_en: methods for detecting brain function

name: Accidents
definition_quote: Accidents like this give researchers clues about brain function.
plain_en: brain injuries give clues about function

name: Phineas Gage
definition_quote: In 1848, a railroad worker named Phineas Gage was involved in an accident that damaged the front part of his brain.
plain_en: brain injury changed his emotions and impulses

name: Lesioning
definition_quote: Lesioning is the removal or destruction of part of the brain.
plain_en: destroying or removing brain tissue

name: Electroencephalogram (EEG)
definition_quote: An electroencephalogram (EEG) detects brain waves.
plain_en: detects and records brain waves

name: Computerized axial tomography (CAT or CT) scan
definition_quote: A computerized axial tomography (CAT or CT) scan is a sophisticated X ray.
plain_en: sophisticated X-ray image of brain

name: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
definition_quote: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is similar to a CAT scan in a way: both scans give you pictures of the brain.
plain_en: magnetic scan producing detailed brain images

name: Positron emission tomography (PET) scan
definition_quote: A positron emission tomography (PET) scan lets researchers see what areas of the brain are most active during certain tasks.
plain_en: shows brain areas active during tasks

name: Functional MRI (fMRI)
definition_quote: Functional MRI (fMRI) is a technology that combines elements of the MRI and PET scans.
plain_en: combines MRI and PET scan elements

name: Brain Structure and Function
definition_quote: When you study the brain, think about three separate major categories or sections: hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain.
plain_en: brain's three sections: hindbrain, midbrain, forebrain

name: Hindbrain
definition_quote: The hindbrain consists of structures located on top of the spinal cord. The hindbrain is our life support system; it controls the basic biological functions that keep us alive.
plain_en: life support; controls basic biological functions

name: Medulla
definition_quote: The medulla is involved in the control of our blood pressure, heart rate, and breathing.
plain_en: controls blood pressure, heart rate, breathing

name: Pons
definition_quote: The pons (located just above the medulla and toward the front) connects the hindbrain with the midbrain and forebrain.
plain_en: connects hindbrain with midbrain and forebrain

name: Cerebellum
definition_quote: The cerebellum coordinates some habitual muscle movements, such as tracking a target with our eyes or moving our fingers when playing the saxophone.
plain_en: coordinates habitual muscle movements

name: Midbrain
definition_quote: In general, your midbrain coordinates simple movements with sensory information.
plain_en: coordinates simple movements with sensory information

name: Reticular formation
definition_quote: One specific structure in the midbrain you should be familiar with is the reticular formation. It is a netlike collection of cells throughout the midbrain that controls general body arousal and the ability to focus our attention.
plain_en: netlike cells controlling arousal and attention

name: Forebrain
definition_quote: Areas of the forebrain control what we think of as thought and reason.
plain_en: brain areas controlling thought and reasoning

name: Thalamus
definition_quote: The thalamus is located on top of the brain stem. It is responsible for receiving the sensory signals coming up the spinal cord and sending them to the appropriate areas in the rest of the forebrain.
plain_en: relays sensory signals to appropriate forebrain areas

name: Hypothalamus
definition_quote: The hypothalamus controls several metabolic functions, including body temperature, sexual arousal (libido), hunger, thirst, and the endocrine system.
plain_en: regulates temperature, hunger, thirst, and endocrine system

name: Amygdala and hippocampus
definition_quote: The amygdala is vital to our experiences of emotion, and the hippocampus is vital to our memory system.
plain_en: amygdala handles emotion; hippocampus handles memory

name: Limbic system
definition_quote: These parts of the brain (thalamus, hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus) are grouped together and called the limbic system because they all deal with aspects of emotion and memory.
plain_en: group of emotion and memory regions

name: Cerebral cortex
definition_quote: When most people think of the human brain, they think of and picture the cerebral cortex. The gray, wrinkled surface of the brain is actually a thin (0.039-inch [1 mm]) layer of densely packed neurons.
plain_en: thin gray wrinkled layer of neurons

name: Pruning
definition_quote: This process, called pruning, forms the complex neural web you now have in your brain.
plain_en: trimming neural connections into complex networks

name: Hemispheres
definition_quote: The cerebral cortex is divided into two hemispheres: left and right.
plain_en: cortex divided into left and right halves

name: Contralateral hemispheric organization
definition_quote: (The idea that each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body is called contralateral hemispheric organization.)
plain_en: each brain side controls the opposite body side

name: Hemispheric specialization (brain lateralization)
definition_quote: This specialization of function in each hemisphere is called hemispheric specialization, or brain lateralization.
plain_en: each hemisphere specializes in different functions

name: Split-brain patients
definition_quote: Most of this research in differences between the hemispheres is done by examining split- brain patients—patients whose corpus callosum (the nerve bundle that connects the two hemispheres, see Figure 4.3) has been cut to treat severe epilepsy.
plain_en: patients whose corpus callosum was cut

name: Association area
definition_quote: Any area of the cerebral cortex that is not associated with receiving sensory information or controlling muscle movements is labeled as an association area.
plain_en: cortex areas neither sensory nor motor

name: Frontal lobes
definition_quote: The frontal lobes are large areas of the cerebral cortex located at the top front part of the brain behind the eyes (see Figure 4.4).
plain_en: cortex at top front of brain

name: Prefrontal cortex
definition_quote: The anterior or front of the frontal lobe is called the prefrontal cortex and is thought to play a critical role in directing thought processes.
plain_en: directs thought, planning, and emotional control

name: Broca’s area
definition_quote: Broca’s area (named for Paul Broca, 1824–1880) is in the frontal lobe and is responsible for controlling the muscles involved in producing speech.
plain_en: controls muscles producing speech

name: Motor cortex
definition_quote: A thin vertical strip at the back of the frontal lobe (farthest from the eyes, see Figure 4.4) is called the motor cortex. This part of the cerebral cortex sends signals to our muscles, controlling our voluntary movements.
plain_en: sends signals controlling voluntary movements

name: Parietal lobes
definition_quote: The parietal lobes are located behind the frontal lobe but still on the top of the brain (see Figure 4.4).
plain_en: cortex behind frontal lobe, top of brain

name: Somatosensory cortex
definition_quote: The parietal lobes contain the somatosensory cortex (also known as the sensory cortex), which is located right behind the motor cortex in the frontal lobe.
plain_en: receives touch information from the body

name: Phantom limb syndrome
definition_quote: One fascinating phenomenon that involves the somatosensory cortex is phantom limb syndrome: if an individual loses a part of their body, like an arm or hand, the person may still perceive sensations from that lost limb because part of their somatosensory cortex is still “mapped” to the missing body part.
plain_en: sensations perceived from missing body part

name: Occipital lobes
definition_quote: Our occipital lobes are at the very back of our brain, farthest from our eyes. This is somewhat counterintuitive since one of the major functions of this lobe is to interpret messages from our eyes in our visual cortex.
plain_en: back of brain; interprets visual messages

name: Temporal lobes
definition_quote: The temporal lobes process sound sensed by our ears.
plain_en: process sound sensed by ears

name: Wernicke’s area
definition_quote: Wernicke’s area is involved with linguistic processing via both written and spoken speech.
plain_en: language processing for written and spoken speech

name: Brain plasticity
definition_quote: Researchers know some of the functions of different areas of the cerebral cortex, but they have also discovered that the brain is somewhat plastic or flexible.
plain_en: brain flexibility to reorganize after damage

name: Consciousness
definition_quote: While you are reading this text, you can probably become aware of your sense of consciousness.
plain_en: awareness of one's own mental state

name: Mere exposure effect
definition_quote: The mere exposure effect (see also Unit 4) occurs when we prefer stimuli we have seen before over novel stimuli, even if we do not consciously remember seeing the old stimuli.
plain_en: prefer familiar stimuli over novel ones

name: Priming
definition_quote: A closely related concept is priming. Research participants respond more quickly and/or accurately to questions they have seen before, even if they do not remember seeing them.
plain_en: prior exposure speeds later responses

name: Blind sight
definition_quote: Another fascinating phenomenon that demonstrates levels of consciousness is blind sight. Some people who report being blind can nonetheless accurately describe the path of a moving object or accurately grasp objects they say they cannot see!
plain_en: blind people accurately sense unseen objects

name: Conscious level
definition_quote: The information about yourself and your environment you are currently aware of.
plain_en: information currently within awareness

name: Nonconscious level
definition_quote: Body processes controlled by your mind that we are not usually (or ever) aware of.
plain_en: body processes outside our awareness

name: Preconscious level
definition_quote: Information about yourself or your environment that you are not currently thinking about (not in your conscious level) but you could be.
plain_en: information retrievable into conscious awareness

name: Subconscious level
definition_quote: Information that we are not consciously aware of but we know must exist due to behavior.
plain_en: unaware information inferred from behavior

name: Unconscious level
definition_quote: Psychodynamic psychologists believe some events and feelings are unacceptable to our conscious mind and are repressed into the unconscious mind.
plain_en: repressed unacceptable feelings and events

name: Psychoactive drugs
definition_quote: Psychoactive drugs are chemicals that change the chemistry of the brain (and the rest of the body) and induce an altered state of consciousness.
plain_en: chemicals changing brain chemistry and consciousness

name: Blood-brain barrier
definition_quote: Normally, the brain is protected from harmful chemicals in the bloodstream by thicker walls surrounding the brain’s blood vessels. This is called the blood-brain barrier.
plain_en: protects brain from harmful blood chemicals

name: Agonists
definition_quote: The drugs that mimic neurotransmitters are called agonists. These drugs fit in the receptor sites on a neuron that normally receive the neurotransmitter and function as that neurotransmitter normally would.
plain_en: drugs mimicking neurotransmitter effects

name: Antagonists
definition_quote: The drugs that block neurotransmitters are called antagonists. These molecules don't fit the receptor sites well enough to substitute for them but do fit well enough to occupy the same space, thereby preventing neurotransmitters or agonists from causing a reaction.
plain_en: drugs blocking neurotransmitter effects

name: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
definition_quote: One example of this kind of drug is Prozac, which is called a “selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor” because it prevents serotonin from being reabsorbed back into the neuron.
plain_en: prevents serotonin reabsorption back into neuron

name: Tolerance
definition_quote: This change causes tolerance, a physiological change that produces a need for more of the same drug in order to achieve the same effect.
plain_en: need more drug for same effect

name: Withdrawal symptoms
definition_quote: Tolerance will eventually cause withdrawal symptoms in users. Withdrawal symptoms vary from drug to drug.
plain_en: uncomfortable effects after stopping drug use

name: Psychological dependence
definition_quote: Persons psychologically dependent on a drug feel an intense desire for the drug because they are convinced they need it in order to perform or feel a certain way.
plain_en: intense psychological desire or craving

name: Physical dependence
definition_quote: Persons physically dependent on a substance have a tolerance for the drug, experience withdrawal symptoms without it, and need the drug to avoid the withdrawal symptoms.
plain_en: body needs drug to avoid withdrawal

name: Stimulants
definition_quote: Stimulants speed up body processes, including autonomic nervous system functions such as heart and respiration rates.
plain_en: speed up body processes and heart rate

name: Depressants
definition_quote: Depressants slow down the same body systems that stimulants speed up.
plain_en: slow down body systems

name: Hallucinogens
definition_quote: Hallucinogens (also sometimes called psychedelics) do not necessarily speed up or slow down the body. These drugs cause changes in perceptions of reality, including sensory hallucinations, loss of identity, and vivid fantasies.
plain_en: cause perceptual changes and hallucinations

name: Reverse tolerance
definition_quote: This effect is sometimes called reverse tolerance because the second dose may be less than the first but cause the same or greater effects.
plain_en: smaller doses cause same or stronger effects

name: Opiates
definition_quote: The opiates all act as agonists for endorphins and thus are powerful painkillers and mood elevators.
plain_en: endorphin agonists; powerful painkillers and mood elevators

name: Sleep deprived
definition_quote: Many studies show that a large percentage of high school and college students are sleep deprived, meaning they do not get as much sleep as their body wants.
plain_en: not getting as much sleep as needed

name: Circadian rhythm
definition_quote: You may be familiar with the term circadian rhythm. During a 24- hour day, our metabolic and thought processes follow a certain pattern.
plain_en: roughly 24-hour biological rhythm

name: Sleep cycle
definition_quote: Our sleep cycle is our typical pattern of sleep.
plain_en: typical pattern of sleep stages

name: Sleep onset
definition_quote: The period when we are falling asleep is called sleep onset.
plain_en: period of falling asleep

name: Alpha waves
definition_quote: Our brain produces alpha waves when we are drowsy but awake.
plain_en: brain waves when drowsy but awake

name: Theta waves
definition_quote: While we are awake and in stages NREM 1 and NREM 2, our brains produce theta waves, which are relatively high-frequency, low-amplitude waves.
plain_en: high-frequency, low-amplitude waves in NREM 1 and 2

name: Sleep spindles
definition_quote: In NREM stage 2, the EEG starts to show sleep spindles, which are short bursts of rapid brain waves.
plain_en: short bursts of rapid brain waves

name: Delta sleep
definition_quote: From there, we move into NREM stage 3, which is sometimes called delta sleep (also called deep or slow- wave sleep) because of the delta waves that exist during these stages.
plain_en: deep slow-wave sleep with delta waves

name: Restoration of resources
definition_quote: This finding indicates that one of the functions of sleep (and the different stages in the sleep cycle) is restoration of resources: sleep is necessary because our body has to rebuild various resources it used while we were awake and active.
plain_en: sleep rebuilds resources used while awake

name: REM sleep
definition_quote: This is REM—rapid eye movement. This sleep stage is sometimes called paradoxical sleep since our brain waves appear as active and intense as they do when we are awake.
plain_en: rapid eye movement; brain waves appear active

name: REM rebound
definition_quote: Individuals deprived of REM sleep will experience REM rebound—experiencing more and longer periods of REM—the next time they are allowed to sleep normally.
plain_en: more REM after REM deprivation

name: Insomnia
definition_quote: Insomnia is far and away the most common sleep disorder, affecting up to 10 percent of the population. An insomniac has persistent problems getting to sleep or staying asleep at night.
plain_en: persistent trouble falling or staying asleep

name: Narcolepsy
definition_quote: Narcolepsy occurs far more rarely than insomnia, occurring in less than 0.001 percent of the population. Narcoleptics suffer from periods of intense sleepiness and may fall asleep at unpredictable and inappropriate times.
plain_en: intense sleepiness; falls asleep at inappropriate times

name: Sleep apnea
definition_quote: Sleep apnea may be almost as common as insomnia and, in some ways, might be more serious. Apnea causes a person to stop breathing for short periods of time during the night.
plain_en: breathing stops briefly during the night

name: Night terrors
definition_quote: Night terrors usually affect young children, and most do not remember the episode when they wake up.
plain_en: children wake from terror, remember nothing

name: Somnambulism (sleepwalking)
definition_quote: The exact causes are not known, but night terrors are probably related in some way to somnambulism (sleepwalking).
plain_en: walking while asleep

name: Dreams
definition_quote: Dreams are the series of storylike images we experience as we sleep.
plain_en: storylike images experienced during sleep

name: Lucid dreams
definition_quote: Some of us even report lucid dreams in which we are aware that we are dreaming and can control the storyline of the dream.
plain_en: aware of dreaming and controlling storyline

name: Activation-synthesis theory of dreaming
definition_quote: The activation-synthesis theory of dreaming looks at dreams first as biological phenomena. Brain imaging proves that our brain is very active during REM sleep. This theory proposes that perhaps dreams are nothing more than the brain’s interpretations of what is happening physiologically during REM sleep.
plain_en: dreams interpret physiological brain activity during REM

name: Information-processing theory of dreaming
definition_quote: The information-processing theory of dreaming suggests that we use dreams to process the events of the day.
plain_en: dreams process events of the day

name: Consolidation theory of dreams
definition_quote: The information-processing theory of dreaming is closely related to the consolidation theory of dreams: one of the functions of dreams might be to help us encode events and information in our short-term memory into our long-term memory.
plain_en: dreams help consolidate short-term into long-term memory

name: Sensation
definition_quote: sensation in more general terms: the activation of our senses (eyes, ears, and so on)
plain_en: activation of the senses

name: Perception
definition_quote: perception as the process of understanding these sensations
plain_en: process of understanding sensations

name: Transduction
definition_quote: These messages go through a process called transduction, which means the signals are transformed into neural impulses.
plain_en: signals transformed into neural impulses

name: Sensory adaptation
definition_quote: sensory adaptation (decreasing responsiveness to stimuli due to constant stimulation)
plain_en: decreasing responsiveness to constant stimulation

name: Sensory habituation
definition_quote: sensory habituation (our perception of sensations is partially due to how focused we are on them)
plain_en: perception depends partly on attention focus

name: Cocktail party effect
definition_quote: If you are talking with a friend and someone across the room says your name, your attention will probably involuntarily switch across the room. (This is sometimes called the cocktail party effect.)
plain_en: involuntarily notice your name across the room

name: Synesthesia
definition_quote: One example is synesthesia, a phenomenon some people experience in which the activation of one sense, like seeing a color, activates another sense, like hearing a specific sound (or vice versa)!
plain_en: one sense activates another sense

name: Prosopagnosia
definition_quote: Prosopagnosia, another rare condition, involves the inability to recognize faces.
plain_en: inability to recognize faces

name: Vision
definition_quote: Vision is the dominant sense in human beings.
plain_en: dominant human sense

name: Retina
definition_quote: The focused inverted image projects on the retina, which is like a screen on the back of your eye.
plain_en: screen at the back of the eye

name: Hues
definition_quote: Different wavelengths within the visible light spectrum appear as different hues.
plain_en: different wavelengths appear as different hues

name: Amplitude
definition_quote: Another important factor is the wave’s amplitude (height), which dictates its intensity.
plain_en: wave height determines intensity

name: Cornea
definition_quote: The reflected light first enters the eye through the cornea.
plain_en: eye's first structure light passes through

name: Pupil
definition_quote: The pupil is like the shutter of a camera.
plain_en: opening controlling amount of light entering

name: Accommodation
definition_quote: Through a process called accommodation, light that enters the pupil is focused by the lens; the lens is curved and flexible so it can change shape to focus the light on the retina.
plain_en: lens changes shape to focus light

name: Transduction
definition_quote: The term transduction refers to the translation of incoming stimuli into neural signals.
plain_en: stimuli translated into neural signals

name: Cones
definition_quote: cones, which are cells that are activated by color
plain_en: retina cells activated by color

name: Rods
definition_quote: rods, which are cells that respond to black and white
plain_en: cells responding to black and white

name: Fovea
definition_quote: At the very center of the retina is an indentation called the fovea that contains the highest concentration of cones.
plain_en: retina center with highest cone concentration

name: Blind spot
definition_quote: The spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina has no rods or cones, so it is referred to as the blind spot.
plain_en: no receptors where optic nerve exits

name: Optic chiasm
definition_quote: The spot where the nerves cross each other is called the optic chiasm.
plain_en: where optic nerves cross

name: Feature detectors
definition_quote: The visual cortex has feature detectors for vertical lines, curves, motion, and many other features of images.
plain_en: neurons responding to specific visual features

name: Theories of color vision
definition_quote: Competing theories exist about how and why we see color.
plain_en: competing explanations of color perception

name: Trichromatic theory
definition_quote: The oldest and simplest theory is trichromatic theory. This theory hypothesizes that we have three types of cones in the retina and that each type detects a different primary color of light: blue, red, or green.
plain_en: three cone types detect red, green, blue

name: Afterimage
definition_quote: If you stare at one color for a while and then look at a white or blank space, you will see a negative color afterimage.
plain_en: complementary color seen after staring

name: Dichromatism
definition_quote: Individuals with dichromatism cannot see either red/green shades or blue/yellow shades.
plain_en: cannot see red-green or blue-yellow shades

name: Opponent-process theory
definition_quote: The opponent-process theory states that the sensory receptors arranged in the retina come in pairs: red/green pairs, yellow/blue pairs, and black/white pairs.
plain_en: color receptors arranged in opposing pairs

name: Pitch
definition_quote: Frequency refers to the length of the waves and determines pitch, which is measured in megahertz.
plain_en: wave frequency determines pitch

name: Loudness
definition_quote: Amplitude is the height of the wave and determines the loudness of the sound, which is measured in decibels.
plain_en: wave amplitude determines loudness

name: Cochlea
definition_quote: The oval window membrane is attached to the cochlea, a structure shaped like a snail’s shell and filled with fluid.
plain_en: snail-shaped fluid-filled inner ear structure

name: Sound localization
definition_quote: In this way, we can determine approximately where a sound originated; this is called sound localization.
plain_en: judging where a sound originated

name: Pitch theories
definition_quote: As with color vision, two different theories describe the two processes involved in hearing pitch: place theory and frequency theory.
plain_en: two theories explaining pitch perception

name: Place theory
definition_quote: Place theory holds that the hair cells in the cochlea respond to different frequencies of sound based on where they are located in the cochlea.
plain_en: hair cells respond based on location

name: Frequency theory
definition_quote: Frequency theory states that we sense pitch because the hair cells fire at different rates (frequencies) in the cochlea.
plain_en: hair cells fire at different rates

name: Conduction deafness
definition_quote: Conduction deafness occurs when something goes wrong with the system of conducting the sound to the cochlea (in the ear canal, eardrum, hammer/anvil/stirrup, or oval window).
plain_en: sound conduction pathway is damaged

name: Nerve deafness
definition_quote: Nerve deafness (or sensorineural deafness) occurs when the hair cells in the cochlea are damaged, usually by loud noise.
plain_en: damaged cochlear hair cells cause deafness

name: Gate control theory
definition_quote: Gate control theory helps explain how we experience pain the way we do. This theory explains that some pain messages have a higher priority than others.
plain_en: some pain messages have higher priority

name: Pain receptors
definition_quote: If touch or temperature receptors are stimulated sharply, a different kind of nerve ending called pain receptors will also fire.
plain_en: nerve endings firing with sharp stimulation

name: Endorphins
definition_quote: Endorphins, or pain-killing chemicals in the body, also swing the gate shut.
plain_en: natural pain-killing chemicals in the body

name: Taste buds
definition_quote: Chemicals from the food we eat (or whatever else we stick into our mouths) are absorbed by taste buds on our tongue (see Figure 6.3).
plain_en: tongue structures absorbing food chemicals

name: Papillae
definition_quote: Taste receptors are located on papillae, which are the bumps you can see on your tongue.
plain_en: visible bumps on the tongue

name: Five different types of tastes
definition_quote: Humans sense five different types of tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami (savory or meaty taste), and oleogutus (taste of fat).
plain_en: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami, fat

name: Supertasters
definition_quote: If all the bumps are packed tightly together, you probably taste food intensely. (These individuals are called supertasters.)
plain_en: densely packed taste buds, intense taste

name: Smell (or Olfaction)
definition_quote: Our sense of smell also depends on chemicals emitted by substances.
plain_en: depends on chemicals emitted by substances

name: Olfactory bulb
definition_quote: These receptor cells are linked to the olfactory bulb (see Figure 6.4), which gathers the messages from the olfactory receptor cells and sends this information to the brain.
plain_en: gathers smell messages, sends to brain

name: Vestibular sense
definition_quote: Our vestibular sense tells us about how our body is oriented in space.
plain_en: body orientation in space

name: Semicircular canals
definition_quote: Three semicircular canals in the inner ear (see Figure 6.2) give the brain feedback about body orientation.
plain_en: inner ear canals giving orientation feedback

name: Kinesthetic sense (kinesthesis)
definition_quote: While our vestibular sense keeps track of the overall orientation of our body, our kinesthetic sense (kinesthesis) gives us feedback about the position and orientation of specific body parts.
plain_en: position and movement of specific body parts

name: Perception
definition_quote: Perception is the process of understanding and interpreting sensations.
plain_en: interpreting and understanding sensations

name: Psychophysics
definition_quote: Psychophysics is the study of the interaction between the sensations we receive and our experience of them.
plain_en: study of sensation and subjective experience

name: absolute threshold
definition_quote: The absolute threshold is the smallest amount of stimulus we can detect.
plain_en: smallest stimulus amount we can detect

name: subliminal
definition_quote: Stimuli below our absolute threshold are said to be subliminal.
plain_en: stimuli below the absolute threshold

name: difference threshold
definition_quote: The difference threshold, sometimes called a just-noticeable difference, is the smallest amount of change needed in a stimulus before we detect a change.
plain_en: smallest detectable change in a stimulus

name: Weber’s law
definition_quote: This threshold is computed by Weber’s law, which states that the change needed is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus.
plain_en: change needed is proportional to original intensity

name: signal detection theory
definition_quote: Signal detection theory investigates the effects of the distractions and interference we experience while perceiving the world.
plain_en: how distractions affect detecting stimuli

name: false positive
definition_quote: A false positive is when we think we perceive a stimulus that is not there.
plain_en: perceiving a stimulus that is not there

name: false negative
definition_quote: A false negative is not perceiving a stimulus that is present.
plain_en: failing to perceive a present stimulus

name: top-down processing
definition_quote: Top-down processing occurs when you use your background knowledge to fill in gaps in what you perceive.
plain_en: using background knowledge to fill perceptual gaps

name: schemata
definition_quote: Our experience creates schemata (also called schema), which are mental representations of how we expect the world to be.
plain_en: mental representations of how the world works

name: perceptual set
definition_quote: Schemata can create a perceptual set, which is a predisposition to perceiving something in a certain way.
plain_en: predisposition to perceive something in a certain way

name: bottom-up processing
definition_quote: Instead of using our experience to perceive an object, we use only the features of the object itself to build a complete perception.
plain_en: building perception from an object's features

name: figure-ground relationship
definition_quote: One of the first perceptual decisions our mind must make is the figure-ground relationship. What part of a visual image is the figure and what part is the ground or background?
plain_en: distinguishing the figure from its background

name: Gestalt psychology
definition_quote: The Gestalt psychology points out that we normally perceive images as groups, not as isolated elements.
plain_en: perceiving images as organized groups

name: Proximity
definition_quote: Objects that are close together are more likely to be perceived as belonging in the same group.
plain_en: nearby objects group together

name: Similarity
definition_quote: Objects that are similar in appearance are more likely to be perceived as belonging in the same group.
plain_en: similar-looking objects group together

name: Continuity
definition_quote: Objects that are arranged in a continuous line or curve (such as a trail or a geometric figure) are more likely to be perceived as belonging in the same group.
plain_en: objects in continuous lines group together

name: Closure
definition_quote: Objects that make up a recognizable image are more likely to be perceived as belonging in the same group even if the image contains gaps that the mind needs to fill in; note that this perception is influenced by top-down processing.
plain_en: mind fills gaps to complete figures

name: constancy
definition_quote: Our ability to maintain a constant perception of an object despite these changes is called constancy.
plain_en: maintaining constant perception despite changing conditions

name: size constancy
definition_quote: We keep a constant size in mind for an object (if we are familiar with the typical size of the object) and know that it does not grow or shrink in size as it moves closer or farther away.
plain_en: knowing object size stays constant across distances

name: shape constancy
definition_quote: Objects viewed from different angles produce different shapes on our retinas, but we know the shape of an object remains constant.
plain_en: knowing shape stays constant across viewing angles

name: brightness constancy
definition_quote: We perceive objects as being a constant color even as the light reflecting off the object changes.
plain_en: perceiving constant color despite changing light

name: stroboscopic effect
definition_quote: A common example of this is the stroboscopic effect, used in movies or flip books. Images in a series of still pictures presented at a certain speed will appear to be moving.
plain_en: still pictures shown rapidly appear moving

name: phi phenomenon
definition_quote: Another example you have probably encountered on movie marquees and with holiday lights is the phi phenomenon. A series of lightbulbs turned on and off at a particular rate will appear to be one moving light.
plain_en: lights blinking in sequence appear moving

name: autokinetic effect
definition_quote: A third example is the autokinetic effect. If a spot of light is projected steadily onto the same place on a wall of an otherwise dark room and people are asked to stare at it, they will report seeing it move.
plain_en: fixed light in dark seems to move

name: depth perception
definition_quote: Without depth perception, we would perceive the world as a two-dimensional flat surface and be unable to differentiate between what is near and what is far.
plain_en: ability to judge distance and three dimensions

name: visual cliff
definition_quote: Researcher Eleanor Gibson used the visual cliff experiment to determine when human infants can perceive depth. An infant is placed onto one side of a glass-topped table that creates the impression of a cliff.
plain_en: glass table creating illusion of a cliff

name: monocular depth cues
definition_quote: monocular depth cues (depth cues that do not depend on having two eyes)
plain_en: depth cues needing only one eye

name: linear perspective
definition_quote: One of the most common cues is linear perspective. If you wanted to draw a railroad track that runs away from the viewer off into the distance, most likely you would start by drawing two lines that converge somewhere toward the top of your paper.
plain_en: converging parallel lines show distance

name: relative size
definition_quote: If you added a drawing of the train, you might use the relative size cue. You would draw the boxcars closer to the viewer as larger than the engine off in the distance.
plain_en: larger nearby, smaller distant objects

name: interposition
definition_quote: A water tower blocking our view of part of the train would be seen as closer to us due to the interposition cue; objects that block the view to other objects must be closer to us.
plain_en: blocking objects are perceived as closer

name: texture gradient
definition_quote: This cue is called texture gradient; we know that we can see details in texture close to us but not far away.
plain_en: near texture clear, far texture blurry

name: shadowing
definition_quote: By shading part of your picture, you can imply where the light source is and thus imply depth and position of objects.
plain_en: shading implies light source and depth

name: binocular depth cues
definition_quote: binocular depth cues (cues that depend on having two eyes)
plain_en: depth cues requiring two eyes

name: retinal disparity
definition_quote: Each of our eyes will view an object from a slightly different angle. The brain receives both images. It knows that if the object is far away, the images will be similar, but the closer the object is, the more disparity there will be between the images coming from each eye.
plain_en: differing eye images provide depth information

name: convergence
definition_quote: The other binocular depth cue is convergence. As an object gets closer to our face, our eyes must move toward each other to keep focused on the object.
plain_en: eyes turn inward for nearby objects

name: perceptual sets
definition_quote: Cross- cultural research demonstrates that some basic perceptual sets are learned from our culture.
plain_en: some perceptual sets learned from culture

name: Muller-Lyer illusion
definition_quote: Line A should look longer even though both lines are actually the same length.
plain_en: equal lines look different lengths

name: noncarpentered cultures
definition_quote: People who come from noncarpentered cultures that do not often use right angles and corners in their building and architecture are not usually fooled by the Muller-Lyer illusion.
plain_en: cultures without right angles in architecture

name: extrasensory perception (ESP)
definition_quote: someone claiming to have “extrasensory perception” is claiming to perceive a sensation “outside” the senses discussed in Unit 1.
plain_en: claiming perception outside the normal senses

name: thinking and creativity
definition_quote: Describing thinking and creativity is one of the most challenging areas in the science of psychology.
plain_en: thinking and creativity are hard to describe

name: concepts
definition_quote: We each have cognitive rules we apply to stimuli from our environment that allow us to categorize and think about the objects, people, and ideas we encounter.
plain_en: mental rules for categorizing objects and ideas

name: prototypes
definition_quote: We may base our concepts on prototypes, or what we think is the most typical example of a particular concept.
plain_en: most typical example of a concept

name: images
definition_quote: Another type of thought, images, are the mental pictures we create in our minds of the outside world.
plain_en: mental pictures of the outside world

name: algorithm
definition_quote: An algorithm is a rule that guarantees the right solution by using a formula or other foolproof method.
plain_en: formula guaranteeing the correct solution

name: heuristic
definition_quote: A heuristic is a rule of thumb—a strategy we can use to make a quick but not necessarily accurate judgment in a situation.
plain_en: quick but not always accurate strategy

name: availability heuristic
definition_quote: Judging a situation based on examples of similar situations that come to mind initially.
plain_en: judging by easily recalled examples

name: representativeness heuristic
definition_quote: Judging a situation based on how similar the aspects are to prototypes the person holds in his or her mind.
plain_en: judging by similarity to mental prototypes

name: overconfidence
definition_quote: Overconfidence is our tendency to overestimate how accurate our judgments are.
plain_en: overestimating the accuracy of our judgments

name: belief bias
definition_quote: Belief bias occurs when we make illogical conclusions to confirm our preexisting beliefs.
plain_en: illogical reasoning to confirm existing beliefs

name: belief perseverance
definition_quote: Belief perseverance refers to our tendency to maintain a belief even after the evidence we used to form the belief is contradicted.
plain_en: keeping beliefs after evidence is contradicted

name: gambler’s fallacy
definition_quote: Another example of a limitation of a heuristic is the gambler’s fallacy: this occurs when we believe that a certain event or outcome is more or less likely to occur because of how often it has recently occurred.
plain_en: thinking recent outcomes change next probability

name: sunk-cost fallacy
definition_quote: The sunk-cost fallacy can also influence our thinking in negative ways. Sometimes we are unwilling to change a course of action because we spent a lot of effort and time trying to make that solution work, even when it becomes clear that the course of action is unlikely to solve the problem.
plain_en: refusing change because of past investment

name: mental set
definition_quote: Mental set (also called rigidity) refers to the tendency to fall into established thought patterns.
plain_en: sticking to established thought patterns

name: functional fixedness
definition_quote: One specific example of rigidity is functional fixedness, the inability to see a new use for an object.
plain_en: cannot see new uses for objects

name: subgoals
definition_quote: Studies show that good problem solvers identify subgoals, which are smaller and more manageable problems they need to solve in order to solve the whole problem.
plain_en: smaller problems solved to solve the whole

name: confirmation bias
definition_quote: Another obstacle to successful problem-solving is confirmation bias. Many studies show that we tend to look for evidence that confirms our beliefs and ignore evidence that contradicts what we think is true.
plain_en: seeking only evidence supporting our beliefs

name: framing
definition_quote: Framing refers to the idea that the same information can be presented in different ways and the method of presentation can drastically change the way we view a problem or an issue.
plain_en: presentation method changes how we judge

name: convergent thinking
definition_quote: convergent thinking, which is thinking pointed toward one solution
plain_en: thinking aimed at one solution

name: divergent thinking
definition_quote: divergent thinking, which is thinking that searches for multiple possible answers to a question.
plain_en: thinking searching for many possible answers

name: models, or explanations, of how memory works
definition_quote: Several different models, or explanations, of how memory works have emerged from memory research.
plain_en: different models explaining how memory works

name: three-box/information-processing model
definition_quote: The principal model of memory is the three-box model, also called the information-processing model or the multi-store model. This model proposes the three stages that information passes through before it is stored (see Figure 9.1).
plain_en: memory model with three processing stages

name: sensory memory
definition_quote: The first stop for external events is sensory memory. It is a holding tank for incoming sensory information.
plain_en: brief holding of incoming sensory information

name: iconic memory
definition_quote: less than a second for visual information (iconic memory)
plain_en: very brief visual sensory memory

name: echoic memory
definition_quote: three to four seconds for auditory information (echoic memory)
plain_en: auditory sensory memory lasting seconds

name: selective attention
definition_quote: We encode what we are attending to or what is important to us.
plain_en: encoding what we attend to or matters

name: cocktail party effect
definition_quote: However, once a sensory message that you knew was important (like someone saying your name or hearing someone shout “Fire!”) entered sensory memory, you switched your attention to that message, and it was encoded into your short-term memory. (This phenomenon is called the cocktail party effect.)
plain_en: important sounds capture attention and get encoded

name: inattentional blindness
definition_quote: We’ve all experienced inattentional blindness: when we fail to perceive something that was in our visual field (and that our eyes probably sensed) because we weren’t paying attention to it and were intensely focused on something else.
plain_en: missing visible things while intensely focused

name: change blindness
definition_quote: A closely related experience is change blindness: sometimes we do not observe an obvious change in our visual world because we are selectively attending to something else and do not perceive that an object or person changed.
plain_en: failing to notice obvious visual changes

name: short-term memory
definition_quote: Everything you are thinking at the current moment is held in your short-term memory, and if you are trying to do something with that information, it’s in your working memory.
plain_en: temporary storage of current thoughts

name: working memory
definition_quote: Working memory is your ability to manipulate items in your short-term memory.
plain_en: ability to manipulate short-term memory items

name: central executive
definition_quote: The central executive—monitors incoming information and determines what other systems should be involved in processing the information.
plain_en: monitors information and directs processing systems

name: visuospatial sketchpad
definition_quote: The visuospatial sketchpad—deals with visual information; this is our “mind’s eye” that we use to visualize the world.
plain_en: mental workspace for visual and spatial information

name: auditory loop
definition_quote: The auditory loop—deals with words or numbers.
plain_en: processes words and numbers

name: maintenance rehearsal
definition_quote: When you get a confirmation code, you probably need to repeat it to yourself until you type it in; this is an example of maintenance rehearsal.
plain_en: repeating information to keep it in short-term

name: elaborative rehearsal
definition_quote: Elaborative rehearsal is a type of effortful processing: it occurs when we focus on putting mental effort into encoding the meaning of a term, an event, a process, and so on.
plain_en: effortful encoding of information's meaning

name: semantic memory
definition_quote: This is closely related to semantic memory, which involves memories related to the significance or meaning of information.
plain_en: memory for the meaning of information

name: long-term memory
definition_quote: Long-term memory is our permanent storage.
plain_en: permanent storage of information

name: episodic memory
definition_quote: Memories of specific events, stored in a sequential series of events.
plain_en: specific events stored in sequence

name: semantic memory
definition_quote: General knowledge of the world, stored as facts, meanings, or categories rather than sequentially.
plain_en: general facts, meanings, and categories stored

name: procedural memory
definition_quote: Memories of skills and how to perform them.
plain_en: memory for performing skills and procedures

name: explicit memories
definition_quote: Explicit memories (also called declarative memories) are what we usually think of first. They are the conscious memories of facts or events we actively tried to remember.
plain_en: conscious memories of facts and events

name: implicit memories
definition_quote: Implicit memories (also called nondeclarative memories) are unintentional memories that we might not even realize we have.
plain_en: unintentional memories we do not realize

name: prospective memory
definition_quote: Yet another type of memory is prospective memory, which is your memory for things you plan to do in the future.
plain_en: remembering things to do in future

name: eidetic memory
definition_quote: Luria and other researchers showed that these rare individuals seem to use very powerful and enduring visual images.
plain_en: rare, vivid, enduring visual images

name: levels of processing model
definition_quote: An alternate way to think about memory is the levels of processing model. This theory explains why we remember what we do by examining how deeply the memory was processed or thought about.
plain_en: memory depends on depth of processing

name: shallowly encoded
definition_quote: If you simply repeat a fact to yourself several times and then write it on your test as quickly as you can, you have only shallowly encoded that fact and you will forget it quickly.
plain_en: only rote repetition, quickly forgotten

name: deeply encoded
