definition_quote: However, if you study the context and research the reasons behind the fact, you have deeply encoded it and will likely recall it later.
plain_en: processing meaning and context for better recall

name: long-term potentiation
definition_quote: At the neurological level, researchers focus on a process called long-term potentiation. Studies show that neurons can strengthen connections between each other.
plain_en: repeated activation strengthens neuronal connections

name: encoding
definition_quote: Encoding is the process by which we put information into our memories, and it can be affected by many factors.
plain_en: process of putting information into memory

name: primacy effect
definition_quote: The primacy effect predicts that we are more likely to recall items presented at the beginning of a list.
plain_en: better recall of list beginnings

name: recency effect
definition_quote: The recency effect is demonstrated by our ability to recall the items at the end of a list.
plain_en: better recall of list ends

name: serial position effect
definition_quote: Together the primacy effect and recency effect demonstrate the serial position effect (also called the serial position curve). This effect is seen when recall of a list is affected by the order of items in a list.
plain_en: list position affects recall

name: method of loci
definition_quote: A well-known example is the method of loci. This method involves using imagery to associate the things you want to remember with various places.
plain_en: linking memories to imagined places

name: spacing effect
definition_quote: One of the most robust findings in memory research is called the spacing effect. Research has consistently demonstrated the benefit of spacing studying out or using what is called distributed practice, as opposed to massed practice.
plain_en: distributed practice beats massed practice

name: chunking
definition_quote: However, this limit can be expanded through a process called chunking. If you want to remember a grocery list with 15 items on it, you should chunk, or group, the items into no more than seven groups.
plain_en: grouping items to remember more

name: mnemonic devices
definition_quote: Most mnemonic devices, which are memory aids, are really examples of chunking.
plain_en: memory aids such as grouping

name: hippocampus
definition_quote: By studying patients with specific brain damage, we know that the hippocampus is important in encoding new memories.
plain_en: brain structure encoding new memories

name: anterograde amnesia
definition_quote: Individuals with damage to the hippocampus might have anterograde amnesia (cannot encode new memories) but can recall events already in memory.
plain_en: cannot form new memories

name: retrograde amnesia
definition_quote: People with retrograde amnesia have a different problem; they are unable to remember information learned before a trauma to the brain.
plain_en: cannot recall events before brain trauma

name: cerebellum
definition_quote: (Studies on animals indicate that procedural memories are stored in the cerebellum.)
plain_en: brain structure storing procedural memories

name: retrieval
definition_quote: The last step in any memory model is retrieval, or getting information out of memory so we can use it.
plain_en: accessing stored information for use

name: recognition
definition_quote: Recognition is the process of matching a current event or fact with one already in memory (e.g., “Have I smelled this smell before?”).
plain_en: matching current stimulus to memory

name: recall
definition_quote: Recall is retrieving a memory with an external cue (e.g., “What does my Aunt Beki’s perfume smell like?”).
plain_en: retrieving memories with external cues

name: retrieval cues
definition_quote: Both rely on retrieval cues, which are stimuli that help people retrieve memories.
plain_en: stimuli that help retrieve memories

name: tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon
definition_quote: This temporary inability to remember information is sometimes called the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon.
plain_en: temporary inability to remember known information

name: semantic network theory
definition_quote: One theory that explains why this might work is the semantic network theory. This theory states that our brain might form new memories by connecting their meaning and context with meanings already in memory.
plain_en: memories connected by meaning and context

name: flashbulb memories
definition_quote: Also called flashbulb memories, these memories are powerful because the importance of the event caused us to encode the context surrounding the event.
plain_en: vivid memories of important events

name: mood-congruent memory
definition_quote: Studies consistently demonstrate the power of mood-congruent memory or the greater likelihood of recalling an item when our current mood matches the mood we were in when the event happened.
plain_en: matching mood makes recall more likely

name: state-dependent memory
definition_quote: State-dependent memory refers to the phenomenon of recalling events encoded while in particular states of consciousness.
plain_en: same consciousness state aids recall

name: constructed memory
definition_quote: A constructed memory (or reconstructed memory) includes false details of a real event or might even be a recollection of an event that never occurred.
plain_en: memory with false or invented details

name: misinformation effect
definition_quote: Studies show that leading questions (questions or statements that purposefully include information or events that never happened—called the misinformation effect) can easily influence us to recall false details, and questioners can create an entirely new memory by repeatedly asking insistent questions.
plain_en: misleading information creates false memory details

name: decay
definition_quote: One cause of forgetting is decay: forgetting because we do not use a memory or connections to a memory for a long period of time.
plain_en: unused memories fade over time

name: relearning effect
definition_quote: If you have to memorize the capitals again, it will take you less time than it did the first time you studied them.
plain_en: relearning forgotten material takes less time

name: interference
definition_quote: Another factor that causes forgetting is interference. Sometimes other information in your memory competes with what you are trying to recall.
plain_en: other memories compete during recall

name: retroactive interference
definition_quote: Learning new information interferes with the recall of older information.
plain_en: new learning interferes with older memories

name: proactive interference
definition_quote: Older information learned previously interferes with the recall of information learned more recently.
plain_en: old learning interferes with newer memories

name: intelligence
definition_quote: Francis Galton was a pioneer in the study of human intelligence and testing.
plain_en: Galton pioneered the study of intelligence

name: psychometricians
definition_quote: Although most teachers are experienced with creating tests, psychometricians are psychologists who specialize in making standardized tests.
plain_en: psychologists specializing in standardized tests

name: standardized test
definition_quote: When we say that a test is standardized, we mean that the test items have been piloted on a similar population of people as those who are meant to take the test (the standardization sample) and that achievement norms have been established.
plain_en: piloted, with norms, on similar people

name: reliability
definition_quote: Reliability refers to the repeatability or consistency of the test as a means of measurement.
plain_en: consistency or repeatability of test results

name: split-half reliability
definition_quote: Split-half reliability involves randomly dividing a test into two different sections and then correlating people’s performances on the two halves.
plain_en: correlation between two halves' scores

name: equivalent-form reliability
definition_quote: The correlation between performance on the different forms of the test is known as equivalent-form reliability.
plain_en: correlation between different test versions

name: test-retest reliability
definition_quote: Finally, test-retest reliability refers to the correlation between a person’s score on one administration of the test with the same person’s score on a subsequent administration of the test.
plain_en: correlation between two test administrations

name: validity
definition_quote: A test is valid when it measures what it is supposed to measure.
plain_en: test measures what it should measure

name: face validity
definition_quote: Face validity refers to a superficial measure of accuracy.
plain_en: superficial appearance of measuring correctly

name: content validity
definition_quote: Content validity refers to how well a measure reflects the entire range of material it is supposed to be testing.
plain_en: covers the full range of material

name: concurrent validity
definition_quote: Concurrent validity measures how much of a characteristic a person has now.
plain_en: measures a characteristic a person has now

name: predictive validity
definition_quote: Predictive validity is a measure of future performance.
plain_en: measures future performance

name: aptitude tests
definition_quote: Aptitude tests measure ability or potential
plain_en: measure ability or potential

name: achievement tests
definition_quote: achievement tests measure what one has learned or accomplished
plain_en: measure acquired knowledge or accomplishments

name: speed tests
definition_quote: Speed tests generally consist of a large number of questions asked in a short amount of time.
plain_en: many questions in little time

name: power tests
definition_quote: The goal of a power test is to gauge the difficulty level of problems an individual can solve.
plain_en: gauges difficulty of problems one can solve

name: group tests
definition_quote: Group tests are administered to many people at a time.
plain_en: administered to many people at once

name: individual tests
definition_quote: Individual tests involve greater interaction between the examiner and the examinee.
plain_en: more examiner and examinee interaction

name: intelligence
definition_quote: Typically, intelligence is defined as the ability to gather and use information in productive ways.
plain_en: capacity to use information productively

name: g
definition_quote: Intelligence can be measured by a single, general ability (g).
plain_en: single general intelligence ability

name: factor analysis
definition_quote: factor analysis, which is a statistical technique that measures the correlations between different items
plain_en: statistical technique measuring item correlations

name: multiple intelligences
definition_quote: Theory of multiple intelligences—the term “intelligence” should be applied to a wide variety of abilities including kinesthetic, musical, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic, verbal, spatial, and mathematical.
plain_en: intelligence includes many different abilities

name: intrapersonal intelligence
definition_quote: Intrapersonal intelligence refers to one’s ability to understand oneself.
plain_en: ability to understand oneself

name: interpersonal intelligence
definition_quote: Interpersonal intelligence, on the other hand, corresponds to a person’s ability to get along with and be sensitive to others.
plain_en: ability to get along with others

name: naturalist intelligence
definition_quote: Finally, naturalist intelligence is found in people gifted at recognizing and organizing the things they encounter in the natural environment.
plain_en: recognizing and organizing things in nature

name: triarchic theory
definition_quote: Triarchic theory of intelligence—people can be intelligent in different ways; they can evidence analytic, practical, and creative intelligence.
plain_en: analytic, practical, and creative intelligence types

name: Componential, or analytic, intelligence
definition_quote: Componential, or analytic, intelligence involves the skills traditionally thought of as reflecting intelligence.
plain_en: skills traditionally seen as intelligence

name: creative intelligence
definition_quote: The second type, experiential or creative intelligence, focuses on people’s ability to use their knowledge and experiences in new and innovative ways.
plain_en: using knowledge creatively in new situations

name: practical intelligence
definition_quote: People with this type of intelligence are what we consider street-smart
plain_en: using knowledge in real situations

name: fluid intelligence
definition_quote: Fluid intelligence refers to our ability to solve abstract problems and pick up new information and skills, while crystallized intelligence involves using knowledge accumulated over time.
plain_en: solving abstract problems and learning new skills

name: crystallized intelligence
definition_quote: crystallized intelligence involves using knowledge accumulated over time.
plain_en: applying knowledge gained over the years

name: EQ
definition_quote: EQ roughly corresponds to Gardner’s notions of interpersonal and intrapersonal intelligence.
plain_en: emotional intelligence matching interpersonal and intrapersonal abilities

name: mental age
definition_quote: Binet came up with the concept of mental age, an idea that presupposes that intelligence increases as one gets older.
plain_en: intelligence level expressed as an age

name: IQ
definition_quote: A person’s IQ score on this test is computed by dividing the person’s mental age by his or her chronological age and multiplying by 100.
plain_en: mental age divided by chronological age, times 100

name: deviation IQ
definition_quote: The Wechsler tests yield IQ scores based on what is known as deviation IQ. The tests are standardized so that the mean is 100, the standard deviation is 15, and the scores form a normal distribution.
plain_en: IQ based on deviation from mean

name: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS)
definition_quote: The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is used in testing adults
plain_en: Wechsler test for adults

name: Bias in testing
definition_quote: Interestingly, researchers seem to agree that although different races and genders may score differently on these tests, the tests have the same predictive validity for all groups.
plain_en: whether tests are fair to different groups

name: nature
definition_quote: Keep in mind that nature refers to the influence of genetics, while nurture stresses the importance of the environment and learning.
plain_en: genetic influence on traits

name: nurture
definition_quote: nurture stresses the importance of the environment and learning.
plain_en: environment and learning influence

name: heritability
definition_quote: Heritability is a measure of how much of a trait’s variation is explained by genetic factors.
plain_en: genetic factors' share of trait variation

name: Flynn effect
definition_quote: Performance on intelligence tests has been increasing steadily throughout the century, a finding known as the Flynn effect.
plain_en: IQ scores rising steadily over time

name: Monozygotic (identical) twins
definition_quote: Monozygotic (identical) twins, who share 100 percent of their genetic material, score much more similarly on intelligence tests than do dizygotic (fraternal) twins, who have, on average, only 50 percent of their genes in common.
plain_en: identical twins score more similarly

name: Head Start
definition_quote: Participation in government programs such as Head Start, meant to redress some of the disadvantages faced by impoverished groups, has been shown to correlate with higher scores on intelligence tests.
plain_en: government program helping disadvantaged children

name: differences within groups
definition_quote: After putting the issue of cause aside, when comparing groups of people on any characteristic, keep in mind that differences within groups generally dwarf differences between groups.
plain_en: within-group differences exceed between-group differences

name: A CAUTIONARY NOTE
definition_quote: Thus, we need to take care not to ascribe too great a meaning to a test score.
plain_en: don't overinterpret a single test score

name: Developmental psychology
definition_quote: Developmental psychologists study how our behaviors and thoughts change over the course of our entire lives, from birth to death (or from conception to cremation).
plain_en: study of behavior and thought changes across lifespan

name: Nature versus nurture
definition_quote: This chapter discusses influences on development from nature (genetic factors) first and then moves on to theories about nurture (environmental factors).
plain_en: heredity versus environment as influences on development

name: Cross-sectional research
definition_quote: Cross-sectional research uses participants of different ages to compare how certain variables may change over the lifespan.
plain_en: compares different ages at one point in time

name: Longitudinal research
definition_quote: Instead of sampling from various age groups as in cross-sectional research, a longitudinal study examines one group of participants over time.
plain_en: follows one group of participants over time

name: Genetics
definition_quote: Our genes also help determine what abilities we are born with, such as our reflexes and our process of developing motor skills.
plain_en: genes shape inborn abilities and motor development

name: Teratogens
definition_quote: Certain chemicals or agents (called teratogens) can cause harm if ingested or contracted by the mother.
plain_en: chemicals or agents that can harm fetus

name: Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS)
definition_quote: Children of alcoholic mothers who drink heavily during pregnancy are at high risk for fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS).
plain_en: severe developmental disorder from heavy prenatal alcohol

name: Fetal alcohol effect
definition_quote: Researchers are also investigating a less severe effect of moderate drinking during pregnancy, fetal alcohol effect.
plain_en: milder effect of moderate drinking during pregnancy

name: Reflexes
definition_quote: All babies exhibit a set of reflexes, which are specific, inborn, automatic responses to certain specific stimuli.
plain_en: inborn automatic responses to specific stimuli

name: Rooting reflex
definition_quote: When touched on the cheek, a baby will turn his or her head to the side where he or she felt the touch and seek to put the object into his or her mouth.
plain_en: baby turns head toward cheek touch

name: Sucking reflex
definition_quote: When an object is placed into the baby’s mouth, the infant will suck on it.
plain_en: infant sucks objects placed in mouth

name: Grasping reflex
definition_quote: If an object is placed into a baby’s palm or foot pad, the baby will try to grasp the object with his or her fingers or toes.
plain_en: baby grasps objects touching palm or foot

name: Moro reflex
definition_quote: When startled, a baby will fling his or her limbs out and then quickly retract them, making himself or herself as small as possible.
plain_en: startled baby flings out then retracts limbs

name: Babinski reflex
definition_quote: When a baby’s foot is stroked, he or she will spread the toes.
plain_en: stroked foot makes baby spread toes

name: Visual cliff
definition_quote: Some researchers develop innovative techniques like the visual cliff to measure what babies can perceive visually.
plain_en: apparatus testing infant depth perception

name: Motor development
definition_quote: Barring developmental difficulties, all humans develop the same basic motor skills in the same sequence, especially our gross motor skills like the examples described in this section.
plain_en: motor skills develop in same sequence

name: Gender roles
definition_quote: Different cultures encourage different gender roles, which are behaviors that a culture associates with a gender.
plain_en: behaviors a culture associates with each gender

name: Biopsychological (Neuropsychological) Theory
definition_quote: Biopsychological psychologists concentrate on the nature element in the nature/nurture combination that produces our gender roles.
plain_en: biological factors explain gender role development

name: Social-Cognitive Theory
definition_quote: Social-cognitive psychologists concentrate on the effects society and our own thoughts about gender have on role development.
plain_en: society and thoughts shape gender roles

name: Gender schema theory
definition_quote: These psychologists focus on the internal interpretations we make about the gender messages we get from our environment (also known as gender schema theory).
plain_en: internal interpretations of environmental gender messages

name: Stage theories
definition_quote: Stage theories are, by definition, discontinuous theories of development.
plain_en: development occurs in distinct discontinuous stages

name: Zone of proximal development
definition_quote: a child’s zone of proximal development is the range of tasks the child can perform independently and those tasks the child needs assistance with.
plain_en: tasks child can do alone versus with help

name: Psychosocial stage theory
definition_quote: He thought that our personality was profoundly influenced by our experiences with others, so he created the psychosocial stage theory. It consists of eight stages, each stage centering on a specific social conflict (see Table 11.2).
plain_en: eight stages each centered on social conflict

name: Autonomy
definition_quote: Autonomy is our control over our own body, and Erikson thought that potty training was an early effort at gaining this control.
plain_en: control over one's own body

name: Inferiority complex
definition_quote: If we realize that we are behind or cannot do as well as our peers, which is having an inferiority complex, we may feel anxious about our performance in that area throughout the rest of the stages.
plain_en: feeling inadequate compared with peers

name: Imaginary audience
definition_quote: Other researchers connect this idea with the tendency of adolescents to think about how they are viewed by an imaginary audience and overestimate how much other people are thinking about or focusing on them.
plain_en: adolescents believe others constantly watch them

name: Schemata
definition_quote: Piaget described how children viewed the world through schemata, cognitive rules we use to interpret the world.
plain_en: cognitive rules used to interpret world

name: Assimilation
definition_quote: Typically, we incorporate our experiences into these existing schemata in a process called assimilation.
plain_en: fitting new experiences into existing schemata

name: Accommodation
definition_quote: Sometimes, information does not fit into or violates our schemata, so we must accommodate and change our schemata.
plain_en: changing schemata when new information does not fit

subheading: Sensorimotor Stage (Birth to Approximately Two Years Old)
name: Object permanence
definition_quote: When babies start to look for or somehow acknowledge that objects do exist when they cannot see them, they have object permanence.
plain_en: objects continue existing when out of sight

subheading: Preoperational Stage (Two to Approximately Seven Years Old)
name: Egocentric
definition_quote: Children in this stage are also egocentric in their thinking since they cannot look at the world from anyone’s perspective but their own.
plain_en: unable to see another person's perspective

subheading: Preoperational Stage (Two to Approximately Seven Years Old)
name: Theory of mind
definition_quote: Modern developmental and cognitive psychologists call the ability to think about and consider the mental states of others the theory of mind.
plain_en: ability to consider others' mental states

subheading: Concrete Operational Stage (Eight to Approximately Twelve Years Old)
name: Conservation
definition_quote: Piaget categorized children as being in the concrete operational stage when they demonstrated knowledge of concepts of conservation, the realization that properties of objects remain the same even when their shapes change.
plain_en: properties stay same despite changes in shape

name: Abstract reasoning
definition_quote: Through abstract reasoning, we can manipulate objects and contrast ideas in our mind without physically seeing them or having real-world correlates.
plain_en: manipulating ideas mentally without concrete objects

name: Metacognition
definition_quote: Also, in the formal operational stage, we gain the ability to think about the way we think; this is called metacognition.
plain_en: thinking about one's own thinking

name: Personal fable
definition_quote: This new ability to think abstractly can lead some adolescents into a different kind of egocentric thinking: they can develop a personal fable, which is a belief that they are unique or different from everyone else, or they can develop an attitude of superiority or invulnerability.
plain_en: belief in own uniqueness and invulnerability

subheading: Criticisms of Piaget: Information Processing Model
name: Information processing model
definition_quote: Information processing points out that our abilities to memorize, interpret, and perceive gradually develop as we age rather than developing in distinct stages.
plain_en: cognitive abilities develop gradually with age

name: Phonemes
definition_quote: Phonemes are the smallest units of sound used in a language.
plain_en: smallest units of sound in language

name: Morpheme
definition_quote: A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaningful sound.
plain_en: smallest meaningful unit of sound

name: Syntax
definition_quote: These words are then spoken or written in a particular order, called syntax.
plain_en: rules for ordering words in sentences

name: Semantics
definition_quote: The meanings of words, and the combinations of words in phrases and sentences, is referred to as semantics.
plain_en: meanings of words and sentences

name: Babbling stage
definition_quote: First, if you have ever been around babies, you know that babies babble. This is often cute, and it is the first stage of language acquisition that occurs about four months of age.
plain_en: first language stage beginning around four months

name: Holophrases
definition_quote: The time during which babies speak in single words (holophrases) is sometimes called the holophrastic stage or one-word stage.
plain_en: one-word stage of language acquisition

name: Telegraphic speech
definition_quote: The next language acquisition stage occurs at around 18 months and is called the telegraphic speech or two-word stage.
plain_en: two-word stage beginning around eighteen months

name: Overgeneralization
definition_quote: This misapplication of grammar rules is called overgeneralization or overregularization.
plain_en: misapplying grammar rules to new cases

name: Language acquisition device
definition_quote: Researcher Noam Chomsky theorized that humans are born with a language acquisition device, the ability to learn a language rapidly as children.
plain_en: inborn ability to learn language rapidly

name: Critical period
definition_quote: He theorized that a critical period (a window of opportunity during which we must learn a skill or our development will permanently suffer) for learning language may exist.
plain_en: limited window when a skill must develop

name: Linguistic relativity hypothesis
definition_quote: Psychologist Benjamin Whorf theorized that the language we use might control, and in some ways limit, our thinking. This theory is called the linguistic relativity hypothesis.
plain_en: language controls and limits our thinking

name: Attachment parenting
definition_quote: Some research focused on how attachment parenting, or the reciprocal relationship between caregiver and child, affects development.
plain_en: reciprocal relationship between caregiver and child

name: Imprinting
definition_quote: Biologist Konrad Lorenz established that some infant animals (such as geese) become attached to (imprint on) individuals or even objects they see during a critical period after birth.
plain_en: infant animals attach to first seen object

name: Contact comfort
definition_quote: Harlow’s studies demonstrated the importance of physical comfort in the formation of attachment to parents.
plain_en: physical comfort fosters attachment to parents

name: Temperament
definition_quote: Some researchers try to investigate the possible influences of attachment experiences on our later temperament— our emotional style or typical way we react to stressful situations.
plain_en: typical emotional style of reacting to stress

name: Secure attachment
definition_quote: Infants with secure attachments (about 66 percent of the participants) confidently explored the novel environment while the parents were present, were distressed when the parents left, and came to the parents when they returned.
plain_en: explores confidently but distressed by parent leaving

name: Avoidant attachment
definition_quote: Infants with avoidant attachments (about 21 percent of the participants) resisted being held by the parents and explored the novel environment.
plain_en: resists being held, avoids parent contact

name: Anxious/ambivalent attachment
definition_quote: Infants with anxious/ambivalent attachments (also called resistant attachments or insecure attachments, about 12 percent of the participants) had ambivalent reactions to the parents.
plain_en: ambivalent anxious reactions toward the parent

name: Ecological systems theory
definition_quote: This theory views human development as a system of relationships that is impacted by our environment.
plain_en: development shaped by nested environmental relationship systems

name: Microsystem
definition_quote: Microsystem: direct interactions between the child and their immediate surroundings, including their caregivers.
plain_en: child's direct interactions with immediate surroundings

name: Mesosystem
definition_quote: The mesosystem acknowledges that each of the five ecological systems interact.
plain_en: interactions among the five ecological systems

name: Exosystem
definition_quote: Exosystem: this system involves indirect influences on the child’s development.
plain_en: indirect environmental influences on child development

name: Macrosystem
definition_quote: Macrosystem: influences of the cultures a child is immersed in will also influence his or her development.
plain_en: cultural influences on a child's development

name: Chronosystem
definition_quote: Chronosystem: times of transition or change that occur over the chronology or timeline of a child’s life that influence development.
plain_en: timing of transitions across child's life

name: Authoritarian parents
definition_quote: Authoritarian parents set strict standards for their children’s behavior and apply punishments for violations of these rules.
plain_en: strict standards enforced through punishment

name: Permissive parents
definition_quote: Permissive parents do not set clear guidelines for their children.
plain_en: few or unclear guidelines for children

name: Authoritative parents
definition_quote: Authoritative parents have set consistent standards for their children’s behavior, but the standards are reasonable and explained.
plain_en: consistent reasonable standards explained to children

name: Learning
definition_quote: Learning is commonly defined as a long-lasting change in behavior resulting from experience.
plain_en: lasting behavior change caused by experience

name: Classical conditioning
definition_quote: As a result, Pavlov deduced the basic principle of classical conditioning (also called associative learning). People and animals can learn to associate neutral stimuli (e.g., sounds) with stimuli that produce reflexive, involuntary responses (e.g., food) and will learn to respond similarly to the new stimulus as they did to the old one (e.g., salivate).
plain_en: neutral stimulus paired with reflexive response

name: Unconditioned stimulus (US or UCS)
definition_quote: The original stimulus that elicits a response is known as the unconditioned stimulus (US or UCS).
plain_en: stimulus naturally eliciting an unlearned response

name: Unconditioned response (UR or UCR)
definition_quote: Food elicits the natural, involuntary response of salivation. This response is called the unconditioned response (UR or UCR).
plain_en: natural involuntary response to unconditioned stimulus

name: Conditioned stimulus (CS)
definition_quote: the bell is no longer a neutral stimulus but, rather, a conditioned stimulus (CS)
plain_en: previously neutral stimulus that now elicits response

name: Conditioned response (CR)
definition_quote: the bell elicits salivation, which is now a conditioned response (CR)
plain_en: learned response to conditioned stimulus

name: Acquisition
definition_quote: This learning is also called acquisition since the animals have acquired a new behavior.
plain_en: learning a new conditioned response

name: Delayed conditioning
definition_quote: Generally, the most effective method of conditioning is to present the CS first and then to introduce the US while the CS is still evident.
plain_en: CS presented before US while still present

name: Trace conditioning
definition_quote: Trace conditioning—Presentation of the CS, followed by a short break, followed by presentation of the US.
plain_en: CS then pause then US

name: Simultaneous conditioning
definition_quote: Simultaneous conditioning—Presentation of the CS and US at the same time.
plain_en: CS and US presented together

name: Backward conditioning
definition_quote: Backward conditioning—Presentation of the US first, followed by presentation of the CS.
plain_en: US presented before the CS

name: Extinction
definition_quote: In psychological terminology, the process of unlearning a behavior is known as extinction.
plain_en: weakening and unlearning a conditioned response

name: Spontaneous recovery
definition_quote: Sometimes, after a conditioned response has been extinguished and no further training of the animals has taken place, the response briefly reappears upon presentation of the conditioned stimulus.
plain_en: extinguished response briefly returns after conditioned stimulus

name: Generalization
definition_quote: This tendency to respond to similar CSs is known as generalization.
plain_en: responding to similar conditioned stimuli

name: Discrimination
definition_quote: Subjects can be trained, however, to tell the difference, or discriminate, among various stimuli. This is called discrimination.
plain_en: learning to distinguish among similar stimuli

name: Aversive conditioning
definition_quote: This example is an illustration of what is known as aversion conditioning. Whereas Pavlov’s dogs were conditioned with something pleasant (food), baby Albert was conditioned to have a negative response to the white rat.
plain_en: pairing neutral stimulus with unpleasant response

name: Higher-order conditioning
definition_quote: Once a CS elicits a CR, it is possible, briefly, to use that CS as a US in order to condition a response to a new stimulus. This process is known as higher-order conditioning or second-order conditioning.
plain_en: using conditioned stimulus to condition new one

name: Taste aversion
definition_quote: If you ingest an unusual food or drink and then become nauseous, you may develop an aversion to the food or drink.
plain_en: aversion to food after nausea

name: Biological preparedness
definition_quote: This type of powerful conditioning may occur because of biological preparedness: we are biologically predisposed to associate nausea with something we ate or drank.
plain_en: biological predisposition to learn certain associations

name: Salient stimuli
definition_quote: Salient stimuli are easily noticeable and therefore create a more powerful conditioned response.
plain_en: noticeable stimuli produce stronger conditioned responses

name: Garcia effect
definition_quote: The ease with which animals learn taste aversions is known as the Garcia effect.
plain_en: animals easily learn taste aversions

name: Operant conditioning
definition_quote: Whereas classical conditioning is a type of learning based on association of stimuli, operant conditioning is a kind of learning based on the association of consequences with one’s behaviors.
plain_en: learning based on consequences of behavior

name: Law of effect
definition_quote: Thorndike put forth the law of effect that states that if the consequences of a behavior are pleasant, the stimulus-response (S- R) connection will be strengthened and the likelihood of the behavior will increase.
plain_en: pleasant consequences strengthen stimulus-response connection

name: Instrumental learning
definition_quote: He used the term instrumental learning to describe his work because he believed the consequence was instrumental in shaping future behaviors.
plain_en: consequences shape future behaviors

name: Reinforcer
definition_quote: Reinforcement is defined by its consequences; anything that makes a behavior more likely to occur is a reinforcer.
plain_en: anything making behavior more likely

name: Positive reinforcement
definition_quote: Positive reinforcement refers to the addition of something pleasant.
plain_en: adding pleasant stimulus strengthens behavior

name: Negative reinforcement
definition_quote: Negative reinforcement refers to the removal of something unpleasant.
plain_en: removing unpleasant stimulus strengthens behavior

name: Escape learning
definition_quote: Escape learning allows one to terminate an aversive stimulus; avoidance learning, on the other hand, enables one to avoid the unpleasant stimulus altogether.
plain_en: learning to terminate aversive stimulus

name: Avoidance learning
definition_quote: avoidance learning, on the other hand, enables one to avoid the unpleasant stimulus altogether.
plain_en: learning to prevent unpleasant stimulus entirely

name: Punishment
definition_quote: By definition, punishment is anything that makes a behavior less likely.
plain_en: anything making behavior less likely

name: Positive punishment
definition_quote: positive punishment (usually referred to simply as punishment), which is the addition of something unpleasant
plain_en: adding unpleasant stimulus reduces behavior

name: Omission training
definition_quote: omission training or negative punishment, which is the removal of something pleasant
plain_en: removing pleasant stimulus reduces behavior

name: Shaping
definition_quote: Shaping reinforces the steps used to reach the desired behavior.
plain_en: reinforcing steps toward desired behavior

name: Chaining
definition_quote: Animals can also be taught to perform several responses successively in order to get a reward. This process is known as chaining.
plain_en: linking successive responses for a reward

name: Discriminative stimulus
definition_quote: Discrimination (also called reinforcement discrimination) would involve teaching the rat to press only a particular bar or to press the bar only under certain conditions (e.g., when a tone is sounded). In this last example, the tone is called a discriminative stimulus.
plain_en: signal indicating reinforcement is available

name: Primary reinforcers
definition_quote: Primary reinforcers are, in and of themselves, rewarding.
plain_en: reinforcers rewarding in themselves

name: Secondary reinforcers
definition_quote: Secondary reinforcers are things we have learned to value such as praise or the chance to play a video game.
plain_en: learned reinforcers such as praise

name: Generalized reinforcer
definition_quote: Money is a special kind of secondary reinforcer, called a generalized reinforcer, because it can be traded for virtually anything.
plain_en: secondary reinforcer exchangeable for many things

name: Token economy
definition_quote: In a token economy, every time people perform a desired behavior, they are given a token.
plain_en: tokens earned for desired behaviors

name: Premack principle
definition_quote: This idea, that the reinforcing properties of something depend on the situation, is expressed in the Premack principle. It explains that whichever of two activities is preferred can be used to reinforce the activity that is not preferred.
plain_en: preferred activity reinforces less preferred activity

name: Continuous reinforcement
definition_quote: When you are first teaching a new behavior, rewarding the behavior each time is best. This process is known as continuous reinforcement.
plain_en: rewarding every target behavior

name: Partial-reinforcement effect
definition_quote: In addition, according to the partial- reinforcement effect, behaviors will be more resistant to extinction if the animal has not been reinforced continuously.
plain_en: intermittent reinforcement makes extinction harder

name: Fixed-ratio (FR) schedule
definition_quote: A fixed-ratio (FR) schedule provides reinforcement after a set number of responses.
plain_en: reinforcement after set number of responses

name: Variable-ratio (VR) schedule
definition_quote: A variable-ratio (VR) schedule also provides reinforcement based on the number of bar presses, but that number varies.
plain_en: reinforcement after varying number of responses

name: Fixed-interval (FI) schedule
definition_quote: A fixed-interval (FI) schedule requires that a certain amount of time elapses before a bar press will result in a reward.
plain_en: reinforcement after fixed time interval

name: Variable-interval (VI) schedule
definition_quote: A variable- interval (VI) schedule varies the amount of time required to elapse before a response will result in reinforcement.
plain_en: reinforcement after varying time intervals

name: Instinctive drift
definition_quote: The tendency for animals to forgo rewards to pursue their typical patterns of behavior is called instinctive drift.
plain_en: animals revert to instinctive behavior over rewards

subheading: The Contingency Model of Classical Conditioning
name: Contiguity model
definition_quote: The Pavlovian model of classical conditioning is known as the contiguity model because it postulates that the more times two things are paired, the greater the learning that will take place.
plain_en: more pairings produce stronger learning

subheading: The Contingency Model of Classical Conditioning
name: Contingency model of classical conditioning
definition_quote: Rescorla’s contingency model of classical conditioning reflects more of a cognitive spin, positing that it is necessary for one event to reliably predict another for a strong association between the two to result.
plain_en: one event reliably predicting another creates association

name: Observational learning
definition_quote: As you are no doubt aware, people and animals learn many things simply by observing others.
plain_en: learning by observing others

name: Species specific
definition_quote: This type of learning is said to be species specific; it occurs only among members of the same species.
plain_en: occurs only among same species members

name: Modeling
definition_quote: Modeling has two basic components: observation and imitation.
plain_en: observation and imitation of behavior

name: Latent learning
definition_quote: Latent means hidden, and latent learning is learning that becomes obvious only once a reinforcement is given for demonstrating it.
plain_en: hidden learning shown only with reward

name: Cognitive map
definition_quote: He suggested they had made a mental representation, or cognitive map, of the maze during the first half of the trials and evidenced this knowledge once it would earn them a reward.
plain_en: mental representation of spatial layout

name: Abstract learning
definition_quote: Abstract learning involves understanding concepts such as tree or same rather than learning simply to press a bar or peck a disk to secure a reward.
plain_en: understanding concepts rather than simple responses

name: Insight learning
definition_quote: Insight learning occurs when one suddenly realizes how to solve a problem.
plain_en: sudden realization of problem solution

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social psychology
definition_quote: Social psychology is a broad field devoted to studying the way that people relate to others.
plain_en: study of how people relate to others

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social cognition
definition_quote: This field applies many of the concepts you learned about in the field of cognition, such as memory and biases, to help explain how people think about themselves and others.
plain_en: using cognitive processes to understand social thinking

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social influence theory
definition_quote: Another key concept is social influence theory, the idea that how people feel and act is affected by the other people around them.
plain_en: others affect how people feel and act

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Attribution theory
definition_quote: Attribution theory tries to explain how people determine the cause of what they observe.
plain_en: how people determine causes of observed behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Dispositional attribution
definition_quote: For instance, if your friend Charley told you he got a perfect score on his math test, you might find yourself thinking that Charley is very good at math. In that case, you have made a dispositional attribution or person attribution.
plain_en: attributing behavior to a person's traits

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Situation attribution
definition_quote: Alternatively, you might attribute Charley’s success to a situational factor, such as an easy test; in that case, you make a situation attribution.
plain_en: attributing behavior to situational factors

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Consistency
definition_quote: Consistency refers to how similarly the individual acts in the same situation over time.
plain_en: how similarly one acts over time

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Distinctiveness
definition_quote: Distinctiveness refers to how similar this situation is to other situations in which we have watched Charley.
plain_en: how similar situation is to other situations

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Consensus
definition_quote: Consensus asks us to consider how others in the same situation have responded.
plain_en: how others in same situation respond

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
definition_quote: Even more interesting is the idea that the expectations we have of others can influence the way those others behave.
plain_en: expectations cause others to behave as expected

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Fundamental attribution error
definition_quote: When looking at the behavior of others, people tend to overestimate the importance of dispositional factors and underestimate the role of situational variables.
plain_en: overestimating dispositional factors when explaining others' behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Actor-observer bias
definition_quote: Whereas the fundamental attribution error focuses on how we explain others’ behavior, the actor-observer bias explains both the actor’s tendency to attribute behavior to situational factors and the observer’s tendency to attribute behavior to dispositional factors.
plain_en: situational for self, dispositional for others

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: False-consensus effect
definition_quote: The tendency for people to overestimate the number of people who agree with them is called the false-consensus effect.
plain_en: overestimating how much others agree with us

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Self-serving bias
definition_quote: Self-serving bias is the tendency to take more credit for good outcomes than for bad ones.
plain_en: claiming credit for good outcomes, denying bad

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Just-world phenomenon
definition_quote: This belief in a just world, known simply as the just-world phenomenon or just-world bias, in which misfortunes befall people who deserve them, can be seen in the tendency to blame victims.
plain_en: belief that people deserve their misfortunes

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Attitude
definition_quote: An attitude is a set of beliefs and feelings.
plain_en: set of beliefs and feelings

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Mere exposure effect
definition_quote: The mere exposure effect states that the more one is exposed to something, the more one will come to like it.
plain_en: familiarity from repeated exposure increases liking

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Elaboration likelihood model
definition_quote: According to the elaboration likelihood model, persuasive messages can be processed through either the central route or the peripheral route.
plain_en: persuasion processed through central or peripheral routes

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Central route to persuasion
definition_quote: The central route to persuasion involves deeply processing the content of the message
plain_en: deep processing of message content

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Peripheral route
definition_quote: The peripheral route, on the other hand, involves other aspects of the message, including the characteristics of the person imparting the message (the communicator).
plain_en: persuasion using cues beyond message content

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: LaPiere study
definition_quote: In 1934, Richard LaPiere conducted an early study that illustrated this difference (see Table 13.2).
plain_en: attitudes do not fully predict behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Cognitive dissonance theory
definition_quote: Cognitive dissonance theory is based on the idea that people are motivated to have consistent attitudes and behaviors.
plain_en: inconsistent attitudes and behaviors create tension

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Foot-in-the-door technique
definition_quote: The foot- in-the-door technique suggests that if you can get people to agree to a small request, they will become more likely to agree to a follow-up request that is larger.
plain_en: small request first, then larger request

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Door-in-the-face technique
definition_quote: The door-in-the-face technique argues that after people refuse a large request, they will look more favorably upon a follow- up request that seems, in comparison, much more reasonable.
plain_en: large request refused, then smaller request

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Norms of reciprocity
definition_quote: People tend to think that when someone does something nice for them, they ought to do something nice in return.
plain_en: people should return favors received

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social responsibility norm
definition_quote: A related concept is the social responsibility norm, the belief that we all should do what we can to make the world and our society a better place.
plain_en: duty to help improve society

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social trap
definition_quote: A social trap is a situation in which the betterment of society requires us all to make some kind of sacrifice but our individual contribution is so small that people often choose to act in their own immediate interest instead of in the larger societal interest.
plain_en: self-interest harms the collective good

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Stereotypes
definition_quote: We all have ideas about what members of different groups are like, and these expectations may influence the way we interact with members of those groups. We call these ideas stereotypes.
plain_en: generalized beliefs about group members

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Prejudice
definition_quote: Prejudice is an undeserved, usually negative, attitude toward a group of people.
plain_en: unjustified, usually negative, attitude toward a group

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Implicit attitude
definition_quote: An explicit attitude is something someone is conscious of, while an implicit attitude is something that may influence someone’s behavior without their being aware of it.
plain_en: unaware attitude influencing behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Ethnocentrism
definition_quote: Ethnocentrism, the belief that one’s culture (e.g., ethnic, racial) is superior to others, is a specific kind of prejudice.
plain_en: believing one's culture is superior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Discrimination
definition_quote: Prejudice is an attitude, but discrimination involves an action.
plain_en: action based on prejudice

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Out-group homogeneity bias
definition_quote: People tend to see members of their own group, the in-group, as more diverse than members of other groups, the out-groups. This phenomenon is often referred to as out-group homogeneity bias.
plain_en: seeing out-group members as all alike

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: In-group bias
definition_quote: In addition, researchers have documented a preference for members of one’s own group, a kind of in-group bias.
plain_en: preference for one's own group

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Categorization
definition_quote: Some psychologists have suggested that people naturally and inevitably magnify differences between their own group and others as a function of the cognitive process of categorization.
plain_en: grouping people and exaggerating group differences

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Contact theory
definition_quote: The contact theory, as its name suggests, states that contact between hostile groups will reduce animosity but only if the groups are made to work toward a goal that benefits all and necessitates the participation of all.
plain_en: cooperative contact between groups reduces hostility

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Superordinate goal
definition_quote: The contact theory, as its name suggests, states that contact between hostile groups will reduce animosity but only if the groups are made to work toward a goal that benefits all and necessitates the participation of all. Such a goal is called a superordinate goal.
plain_en: goal requiring all groups to cooperate

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Instrumental aggression
definition_quote: Instrumental aggression is when the aggressive act is intended to secure a particular end.
plain_en: aggression to achieve a specific goal

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Hostile aggression
definition_quote: Hostile aggression, on the other hand, has no such clear purpose.
plain_en: aggression without clear purpose

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Thanatos
definition_quote: Freud linked aggression to Thanatos, the death instinct.
plain_en: death instinct linked to aggression

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Frustration-aggression hypothesis
definition_quote: One of the most influential theories, however, is known as the frustration-aggression hypothesis. This hypothesis holds that the feeling of frustration makes aggression more likely.
plain_en: frustration makes aggression more likely

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Bobo doll experiment
definition_quote: Another common theory is that the exposure to aggressive models makes people aggressive as illustrated by Bandura, Ross, and Ross’s (1963) classic Bobo doll experiment.
plain_en: exposure to aggressive models increases aggression

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Prosocial behavior
definition_quote: Although social psychologists have devoted a lot of time and effort to studying antisocial behavior, they have also studied the factors that make people more likely to help one another. Such helping behavior is termed prosocial behavior.
plain_en: helping behavior benefiting others

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Bystander intervention
definition_quote: Much of the research in this area has focused on bystander intervention, the conditions under which people nearby are more and are less likely to help someone in trouble.
plain_en: conditions under which bystanders help

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Bystander effect
definition_quote: Counterintuitively, the larger the number of people who witness an emergency situation, the less likely any one is to intervene. This finding is known as the bystander effect.
plain_en: more witnesses means less helping

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Diffusion of responsibility
definition_quote: One explanation for this phenomenon is called diffusion of responsibility. The larger the group of people who witness a problem, the less responsible any one individual feels to help.
plain_en: larger groups weaken individual responsibility

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Pluralistic ignorance
definition_quote: Another factor contributing to the bystander effect is known as pluralistic ignorance. People seem to decide what constitutes appropriate behavior in a situation by looking to others.
plain_en: using others' reactions to define appropriate behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Similarity
definition_quote: Although conventional wisdom holds that opposites attract, psychological research indicates that we are drawn to people who are similar to us, those who share our attitudes, backgrounds, and interests.
plain_en: attraction to people sharing our attitudes

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Proximity
definition_quote: Proximity means nearness.
plain_en: nearness promotes attraction

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Reciprocal liking
definition_quote: Thus, the more someone likes you, the more you will probably like that person.
plain_en: liking increases when it is returned

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Self-disclosure
definition_quote: One self-discloses when one shares a piece of personal information with another.
plain_en: sharing personal information with another

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social facilitation
definition_quote: This phenomenon, that the presence of others improves task performance, is known as social facilitation.
plain_en: others' presence improves task performance

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social impairment
definition_quote: Later studies, however, found that when the task being observed was a difficult one rather than a simple, well-practiced skill, being watched by others actually hurt performance, a finding known as social impairment.
plain_en: being watched hurts difficult task performance

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Upward social comparison
definition_quote: Upward social comparison is when we compare ourselves to people doing better than we are
plain_en: comparing self with people doing better

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Downward social comparison
definition_quote: downward social comparison is when we compare ourselves to people doing worse than we are
plain_en: comparing self with people doing worse

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Relative deprivation theory
definition_quote: Relative deprivation theory explains that people tend to feel less satisfied with their lives when they engage in a lot of upward social comparison.
plain_en: upward comparison lowers life satisfaction

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Conformity
definition_quote: Conformity is the tendency of people to go along with the views or actions of others.
plain_en: going along with others' views or actions

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Normative social influence
definition_quote: Normative social influence is when people conform for social reasons—to belong to the group.
plain_en: conforming to belong to the group

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Informational social influence
definition_quote: On the other hand, informational social influence leads to conformity because people think the group knows best.
plain_en: conforming because the group knows best

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Obedience
definition_quote: Although conformity involves following a group without being explicitly told to do so, obedience studies have focused on participants’ willingness to do what another asks them to do.
plain_en: willingness to do what authority asks

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Norms
definition_quote: All groups have norms, which are rules about how group members should act.
plain_en: rules about how members should act

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Social loafing
definition_quote: Social loafing is the phenomenon when individuals do not put in as much effort when acting as part of a group as they do when acting alone.
plain_en: less effort when working in groups

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Group polarization
definition_quote: Group polarization is the tendency of a group to make more extreme decisions than the group members would make individually.
plain_en: groups make more extreme decisions than individuals

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Groupthink
definition_quote: Groupthink, a term coined by Irving Janis, describes the tendency for some groups to make bad decisions. Groupthink occurs when group members suppress their reservations about the ideas supported by the group.
plain_en: suppressing doubts leads to bad decisions

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Deindividuation
definition_quote: This loss of self-restraint occurs when group members feel anonymous and aroused, and this phenomenon is known as deindividuation.
plain_en: anonymity and arousal reduce self-restraint

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Zimbardo’s prison experiment
definition_quote: One famous experiment that showed not only how such conditions can cause people to deindividuate but also the effect of roles and the situation in general is Philip Zimbardo’s prison experiment (see Table 13.2).
plain_en: role-playing can make people cruel

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Personality
definition_quote: Psychologists define personality as the unique attitudes, behaviors, and emotions that characterize a person.
plain_en: unique attitudes, behaviors, emotions characterizing a person

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Type A
definition_quote: Type A people tend to feel a sense of time pressure and are easily angered.
plain_en: time-pressured and easily angered

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Type B
definition_quote: Type B individuals, on the other hand, tend to be relaxed and easygoing.
plain_en: relaxed and easygoing

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Id
definition_quote: The id is in the unconscious and contains instincts and psychic energy.
plain_en: unconscious instincts and psychic energy

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Ego
definition_quote: The ego follows the reality principle, which means its job is to negotiate between the desires of the id and the limitations of the environment.
plain_en: negotiates between id and reality

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Superego
definition_quote: Around the age of five, children begin to develop a conscience and to think about what is right and wrong. This sense of conscience, according to Freud, is their superego.
plain_en: conscience about right and wrong

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Defense mechanisms
definition_quote: The ego uses defense mechanisms to help protect the conscious mind.
plain_en: protect conscious mind from threatening feelings

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Repression
definition_quote: Blocking thoughts out from conscious awareness.
plain_en: blocking thoughts from conscious awareness

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Denial
definition_quote: Not accepting the ego-threatening truth.
plain_en: refusing to accept threatening truth

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Displacement
definition_quote: Redirecting one’s feelings toward another person or object.
plain_en: redirecting feelings toward another person or object

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Projection
definition_quote: Believing that the feelings one has toward someone else are actually held by the other person and directed at oneself.
plain_en: attributing one's own feelings to others

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Reaction Formation
definition_quote: Expressing the opposite of how one truly feels.
plain_en: expressing opposite of true feelings

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Regression
definition_quote: Returning to an earlier, comforting form of behavior.
plain_en: returning to earlier comforting behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Rationalization
definition_quote: Coming up with a beneficial result of an undesirable occurrence.
plain_en: finding benefits in undesirable outcomes

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Intellectualization
definition_quote: Undertaking an academic, unemotional study of a topic.
plain_en: academic, unemotional analysis of a topic

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Sublimation
definition_quote: Channeling one’s frustration toward a different goal.
plain_en: channeling frustration toward a different goal

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Collective unconscious
definition_quote: The collective unconscious is passed down through the species and, according to Jung, explains certain similarities we see among cultures.
plain_en: inherited unconscious shared by all humans

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Archetypes
definition_quote: The collective unconscious contains archetypes that Jung defined as universal concepts we all share as part of the human species.
plain_en: universal concepts shared by humanity

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Inferiority
definition_quote: Adler believed that people are motivated by the fear of failure, which he termed inferiority, and the desire to achieve, which he called superiority.
plain_en: fear of failure driving behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Projective tests
definition_quote: Psychodynamic theorists may use projective tests to try to delve into the unconscious. These tests involve asking people to interpret ambiguous stimuli.
plain_en: interpreting ambiguous stimuli to reveal unconscious

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Rorschach inkblot test
definition_quote: For instance, the Rorschach inkblot test involves showing people a series of inkblots and asking them to describe what they see.
plain_en: describing what one sees in inkblots

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Thematic apperception test (TAT)
definition_quote: The thematic apperception test (TAT) consists of several cards, each of which contains a picture of a person or people in an ambiguous situation.
plain_en: stories about ambiguous picture situations

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Determinism
definition_quote: Determinism is the belief that what happens is dictated by what has happened in the past.
plain_en: past events dictate what happens

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Free will
definition_quote: Neither theory supports the existence of free will, which is an individual’s ability to choose his or her own destiny.
plain_en: ability to choose one's own destiny

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Third force
definition_quote: This perspective is often referred to as the third force because it arose in opposition to the determinism so central to both psychoanalytic and behaviorist models.
plain_en: humanistic psychology opposing psychoanalysis and behaviorism

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Self-concept
definition_quote: Self-concept is a person’s global feeling about himself or herself.
plain_en: global feeling about oneself

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Self-actualization
definition_quote: He believed that people are motivated to reach their full potential or self- actualize.
plain_en: reaching one's full potential

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Unconditional positive regard
definition_quote: Unconditional positive regard is a kind of blanket acceptance.
plain_en: blanket acceptance without conditions

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Traits
definition_quote: Trait theorists believe that we can describe people’s personalities by specifying their main characteristics, or traits.
plain_en: main characteristics describing personality

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Nomothetic approach
definition_quote: Some trait theorists believe that the same basic set of traits can be used to describe all people’s personalities. Such a belief characterizes a nomothetic approach.
plain_en: same traits describe all people

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: 16 PF
definition_quote: Raymond Cattell developed the 16 PF (personality factor) test to measure what he believed were the 16 basic traits present in all people, albeit to different degrees.
plain_en: Cattell's test measuring sixteen basic traits

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Big Five personality traits
definition_quote: More recently, Paul Costa and Robert McCrae have proposed that personality can be described using the Big Five personality traits: extroversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, openness to experience, and emotional stability (or neuroticism).
plain_en: five dimensions describing personality

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Factor analysis
definition_quote: Factor analysis allows researchers to use correlations among traits to see which traits cluster together as factors.
plain_en: correlations reveal traits clustering together

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Idiographic theorists
definition_quote: Other trait theorists, called idiographic theorists, assert that using the same set of terms to classify all people is impossible.
plain_en: same traits cannot describe everyone

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Cardinal dispositions
definition_quote: He suggested that a small number of people are so profoundly influenced by one trait that it plays a pivotal role in virtually everything they do. He referred to such traits as cardinal dispositions.
plain_en: one trait dominates nearly all behavior

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Central dispositions
definition_quote: As their names indicate, central dispositions have a larger influence on personality than secondary dispositions.
plain_en: traits with larger influence on personality

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Reciprocal determinism
definition_quote: His model is based on the idea of reciprocal determinism, also known as triadic reciprocality. These terms essentially mean that each of these three factors influences both of the other two in a constant, looplike fashion.
plain_en: person, environment, behavior mutually influence each other

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Self-efficacy
definition_quote: People with high self-efficacy are optimistic about their own ability to get things done, whereas people with low self-efficacy feel a sense of powerlessness.
plain_en: optimism about one's ability to succeed

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Locus of control
definition_quote: A person can be described as having either an internal or an external locus of control.
plain_en: belief about controlling one's destiny

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Internal locus of control
definition_quote: People with an internal locus of control feel as if they are responsible for what happens to them.
plain_en: believing one controls what happens

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: External locus of control
definition_quote: Conversely, people with an external locus of control generally believe that luck and other forces outside of their own control determine their destinies.
plain_en: luck and outside forces determine destiny

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Explanatory style
definition_quote: We can also differentiate people by their explanatory style—the kind of attributions they make about the things that happen to them.
plain_en: attributions one makes about events

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Optimistic explanatory style
definition_quote: Some people have an optimistic explanatory style, which leads them to make internal, global, and stable attributions for good things that happen to them and external, specific, and unstable attributions for bad experiences.
plain_en: good events internal, bad events external

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Personality inventories
definition_quote: Personality inventories are essentially questionnaires that ask people to provide information about themselves.
plain_en: questionnaires asking people about themselves

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: MMPI-2
definition_quote: The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI-2) is one of the most widely used self-report instruments.
plain_en: widely used self-report personality test

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Barnum effect
definition_quote: Research has demonstrated that people have the tendency to see themselves in vague, stock descriptions of personality.
plain_en: seeing oneself in vague stock descriptions

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Motivation
definition_quote: Motivations are feelings or ideas that cause us to act toward a goal.
plain_en: feelings or ideas causing goal-directed action

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Instincts
definition_quote: If you have pets, you know that different animals are born with instincts, which are automatic behaviors performed in response to specific stimuli.
plain_en: automatic behaviors triggered by specific stimuli

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Drive reduction theory
definition_quote: One early theory about how our physiology motivates us was drive reduction theory, the theory that our behavior is motivated by biological needs.
plain_en: behavior motivated by biological needs

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Need
definition_quote: A need is one of our requirements for survival, such as food, water, or shelter.
plain_en: survival requirement like food or shelter

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Drive
definition_quote: A drive is our impulse to act in a way that satisfies this need.
plain_en: impulse to satisfy a need

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Homeostasis
definition_quote: Our body seeks homeostasis, which is a balanced internal state.
plain_en: balanced internal state

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Primary drives
definition_quote: Primary drives are biological needs, like thirst.
plain_en: innate biological needs like thirst

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Secondary drives
definition_quote: Secondary drives are learned drives.
plain_en: learned drives

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Arousal theory
definition_quote: Some motivations that seem to violate biological theories of motivation can be explained by arousal theory (or sensation- seeking theory), which states that we seek an optimum level of excitement or arousal.
plain_en: seeking optimum excitement or arousal

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Yerkes-Dodson law
definition_quote: In general, most of us perform best with an optimal level of arousal, although this varies with different activities.
