We might perform well at an easy task with a very high level of arousal, but the same high level of arousal would prevent us from performing well on a difficult task.
plain_en: optimal arousal depends on task difficulty

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Opponent-process theory
definition_quote: However, the theory states that we eventually feel an opponent process, meaning a motivation to return to our baseline, neutral state.
plain_en: motivation to return to baseline state

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Incentives
definition_quote: Incentives are stimuli that we are drawn to due to learning.
plain_en: learned stimuli that attract us

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Self-determination theory
definition_quote: Self-determination research indicates that three elements are related to intrinsic motivations involved in what they call self- determination: autonomy, competence, and relatedness.
plain_en: intrinsic motivation involves autonomy, competence, relatedness

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Autonomy
definition_quote: Autonomy is the belief that we have the power to make choices that are important to us.
plain_en: belief one can make important choices

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Competence
definition_quote: Competence is the belief that we have the skills and knowledge needed to accomplish tasks important to us.
plain_en: belief one has skills and knowledge

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Relatedness
definition_quote: Relatedness is our ability to form relationships with others who are important to us.
plain_en: forming relationships with important others

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Hypothalamus
definition_quote: The hypothalamus monitors and helps to control body chemistry (including the ratio of glucose and insulin) and makes us feel hungry when we need to eat.
plain_en: monitors body chemistry, triggers hunger

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Lateral hypothalamus
definition_quote: The lateral hypothalamus (hunger center), when stimulated, causes the animal to eat.
plain_en: hunger center; stimulation causes eating

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Ventromedial hypothalamus
definition_quote: Another part of the hypothalamus, the ventromedial hypothalamus (satiety center), causes the animal to stop eating when it is stimulated.
plain_en: satiety center; stimulation stops eating

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Ghrelin
definition_quote: Ghrelin influences short-term hunger; it’s produced in the stomach and communicates hunger to the brain.
plain_en: stomach hormone signaling short-term hunger

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Leptin
definition_quote: Leptin is produced by fat cells and signals the brain that you have sufficient stored energy and thus are not hungry.
plain_en: fat-cell signal of stored energy

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Set-point theory
definition_quote: Set-point theory describes how the hypothalamus might decide what impulse to send. This theory states that the hypothalamus wants to maintain a certain optimum body weight.
plain_en: hypothalamus maintains optimum body weight

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Externals
definition_quote: For example, research indicates that some of us (called externals) are more motivated to eat by external food cues, such as attractiveness or availability of food.
plain_en: people motivated by external food cues

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Internals
definition_quote: Others (called internals) are less affected by the presence and presentation of food and respond more often to internal hunger cues.
plain_en: people responding to internal hunger cues

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Garcia effect
definition_quote: This is caused by the Garcia effect and occurs whenever nausea is paired with either food or drink.
plain_en: nausea paired with food causes aversion

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Bulimia
definition_quote: People with bulimia eat large amounts of food in a short period of time (binging) and then get rid of the food (purging) by vomiting, exercising excessively, or using laxatives.
plain_en: binging then purging food

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Anorexia nervosa
definition_quote: People with anorexia starve themselves to below 85 percent of their normal body weight and refuse to eat due to their obsession with weight.
plain_en: starvation from obsession with weight

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Sexual response cycle
definition_quote: The famous lab studies done by William Masters and Virginia Johnson documented the sexual response cycle in men and women.
plain_en: four stages of sexual response

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Refractory period
definition_quote: Male systems experience a refractory period—a time period that must elapse before another orgasm.
plain_en: recovery time before another orgasm

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Sexual desire
definition_quote: Sexual desire can be present even when the capability to have sex is lost.
plain_en: desire persists despite lost capability

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Kinsey Reports
definition_quote: Researchers (like Alfred Kinsey, who documented the variety of human sexual behaviors in the famous Kinsey Reports from the 1940s and 1950s) have been able to dispel some common myths about sexuality.
plain_en: documented variety of human sexual behaviors

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Sexual orientation
definition_quote: Studies show that gay and lesbian sexual orientation is not related to traumatic childhood experiences, parenting styles, the quality of relationships with parents, masculinity or femininity, or the sexual orientation of our parents.
plain_en: not caused by parenting or childhood

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Achievement motivation
definition_quote: Achievement motivation examines our desires to master complex tasks and knowledge and to reach personal goals.
plain_en: desire to master tasks and goals

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Extrinsic motivations
definition_quote: Extrinsic motivations are rewards that we get for accomplishments from outside ourselves (for example, grades, salary, and so on).
plain_en: rewards from outside oneself

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Intrinsic motivations
definition_quote: Intrinsic motivations are rewards we get internally, such as enjoyment or satisfaction.
plain_en: internal rewards like enjoyment

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Theory X
definition_quote: Theory X Managers believe that employees will work only if rewarded with benefits or threatened with punishment.
plain_en: managers believe employees need rewards or punishment

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Theory Y
definition_quote: Theory Y Managers believe that employees are internally motivated to do good work and policies should encourage this internal motive.
plain_en: managers believe employees are internally motivated

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Approach-approach conflict
definition_quote: The first, named an approach-approach conflict, occurs when you must choose between two desirable outcomes.
plain_en: choosing between two desirable outcomes

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Avoidance-avoidance conflict
definition_quote: Another type of conflict, an avoidance-avoidance conflict, occurs when you must choose between two unattractive outcomes.
plain_en: choosing between two unattractive outcomes

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Approach-avoidance conflict
definition_quote: An approach-avoidance conflict exists when one event or goal has both attractive and unattractive features.
plain_en: goal has attractive and unattractive features

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Multiple approach-avoidance conflicts
definition_quote: Finally, people experience multiple approach-avoidance conflicts. In these, you must choose between two or more things, each of which has both desirable and undesirable features.
plain_en: choosing among options each having pros and cons

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
subheading: What Comes First—The Emotion or the Physiological Change?
name: James-Lange theory
definition_quote: They theorized that we feel emotion because of biological changes caused by stress.
plain_en: physiological changes cause emotional experience

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
subheading: What Comes First—The Emotion or the Physiological Change?
name: Facial feedback hypothesis
definition_quote: The facial feedback hypothesis is a related idea that suggests that we infer our emotions from our facial expressions.
plain_en: inferring emotions from facial expressions

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
subheading: What Comes First—The Emotion or the Physiological Change?
name: Cannon-Bard theory
definition_quote: They theorized that the biological change and the cognitive awareness of the emotional state occur simultaneously.
plain_en: physiological change and emotion occur simultaneously

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Two-factor theory
definition_quote: Schachter pointed out that both our physical responses and our cognitive appraisal of them (our mental interpretations) combine to cause any particular emotional response.
plain_en: arousal plus cognitive label creates emotion

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Broaden-and-build theory
definition_quote: Another theory of emotion known as the broaden-and-build theory focuses specifically on the power and potential of positive emotions. This theory contends that positive emotions facilitate a playful and experimental mindset, which makes it easier for people to expand their social interactions and try new activities.
plain_en: positive emotions expand thinking and interactions

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Facial expressions
definition_quote: No matter what culture we grew up in, we are likely to use the same facial expressions for basic emotions like happiness, sadness, anger, disgust, surprise, and fear.
plain_en: basic emotion expressions are culturally universal

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Sociobiology
definition_quote: This area of research (sometimes called sociobiology) indicates that the facial expressions we make for basic emotions may be an innate part of our physiological makeup.
plain_en: innate physiological basis for expressions

unit: Unit 4: Social Psychology, Personality, Motivation, and Emotion
name: Display rules
definition_quote: On the other hand, researchers have documented some differences in how people express emotion. One cause is thought to be different cultural display rules.
plain_en: cultural rules governing emotional expression

name: Health
definition_quote: Health is an important area of interest for psychologists.
plain_en: physical and mental health matter to psychologists

name: Psychological factors
definition_quote: Psychological factors can affect physical factors as well as mental ones, and psychologists study how to encourage people to live healthy lives, manage stress, grow emotionally, and deal with mental illness.
plain_en: psychological factors influence physical health

name: Stress
definition_quote: The term stress can refer to either certain life events (stressors) or how we react to these changes in the environment (stress reactions).
plain_en: life events or our reactions to them

name: social readjustment rating scale (SRRS)
definition_quote: Their social readjustment rating scale (SRRS) measured stress using life change units (LCUs).
plain_en: scale measuring stress using life change units

name: life change units (LCUs)
definition_quote: Different changes in life were assigned different LCUs; making a career change would be counted as more LCUs than moving to a new apartment.
plain_en: points assigned to different life changes

name: general adaptation syndrome (GAS)
definition_quote: Hans Selye’s general adaptation syndrome (GAS) describes the general response humans and other animals have to a stressful event.
plain_en: Selye's general bodily response to stressful events

name: Alarm reaction
definition_quote: Our heart rate increases, and blood is diverted away from other body functions to muscles that are needed to react.
plain_en: heart rate rises, blood goes to muscles

name: Resistance
definition_quote: Our body remains physiologically ready (high heart rate, and so on). Hormones are released to maintain this state of readiness.
plain_en: body stays physiologically ready during ongoing stress

name: Exhaustion
definition_quote: If the resistance stage lasts too long, our body can deplete its resources.
plain_en: body's resources depleted after prolonged resistance

name: tend-and-befriend theory
definition_quote: Some people successfully manage stress by actively seeking ways to tend to their own self-care needs and attend to the needs of friends and family members.
plain_en: managing stress by caring for self and others

name: emotion-focused coping
definition_quote: Some people use specific stress management techniques such as meditation/mindfulness exercises, breathing techniques, or combining these stress management techniques with medications prescribed by clinical psychologists.
plain_en: managing emotions through meditation and breathing

name: perceived control
definition_quote: Control over events tends to lessen stress, while a perceived lack of control generally makes the event more stressful.
plain_en: believing one can control events reduces stress

name: Positive psychology
definition_quote: The field of positive psychology emerged in the 1990s to counter what some saw as the overly negative focus of psychology on human error, weakness, and sickness.
plain_en: studies human strengths, virtues, and happiness

name: subjective well-being
definition_quote: One area studied by positive psychologists is subjective well-being, which is a sense of how satisfied a person is with their life overall.
plain_en: how satisfied a person feels with life

name: character strengths
definition_quote: Positive psychology researchers investigate how aspects of personality they call character strengths or virtues can be measured and how using these strengths relates to life satisfaction and achievement.
plain_en: measurable positive personality traits and virtues

name: six core virtues
definition_quote: These researchers identify six core virtues that seem to be valued across all major religions and philosophies: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance, and transcendence.
plain_en: six virtues valued across cultures and philosophies

name: well-being
definition_quote: Well-being refers to our perception of how effectively we function in our personal lives and our role in the groups to which we belong.
plain_en: perception of functioning effectively in life and groups

name: gratitude
definition_quote: Practicing gratitude (by expressing thankfulness toward others verbally or in writing) is associated with increases in our perceptions of happiness and satisfaction in life
plain_en: expressing thankfulness toward others increases happiness

name: resilience
definition_quote: Studies indicate that some people are more able to adapt effectively when faced with trauma and extreme stress and that some people experience post-traumatic growth after these intensely negative experiences.
plain_en: adapting well after trauma and extreme stress

name: post-traumatic growth
definition_quote: One concept positive psychologists talk about with regard to stress and difficult situations is post-traumatic growth, which is the ability to construct a meaningful experience in response to a period of trauma.
plain_en: finding meaning and growth after trauma

name: Psychological disorders
definition_quote: Psychological disorders may manifest in a person’s behavior and/or thoughts.
plain_en: disorders visible in behavior or thinking

name: abnormal psychology
definition_quote: The field of psychological disorders (or abnormal psychology) encompasses the study of relatively common problems such as depression, substance abuse, and learning difficulties as well as the study of fairly rare, and particularly severe, disorders such as bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.
plain_en: field studying psychological disorders and their treatment

name: Psychological disorder
definition_quote: Disorders are often characterized by causing dysfunction, by resulting in distress, and as being deviant (different) from what is typical.
plain_en: dysfunction, distress, and deviance from typical behavior

name: insanity
definition_quote: The reason behind the legal definition of insanity is to differentiate between those people who can be held entirely responsible for their crimes (the sane) and those people who, because of a psychological disorder, cannot be held fully responsible for their actions.
plain_en: legal concept judging criminal responsibility

name: International Classification of Mental Disorders (ICD)
definition_quote: The World Health Organization (WHO) created the International Classification of Mental Disorders (ICD) for this purpose, and the American Psychiatric Association uses the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM).
plain_en: World Health Organization's mental disorder classification

name: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)
definition_quote: The DSM, as its name suggests, provides a way for psychologists to diagnose their patients.
plain_en: American manual used to diagnose mental disorders

name: etiologies
definition_quote: These resources do not include much discussion of the causes (also called etiologies) or treatments of the various disorders, because adherents to each of the psychological perspectives disagree (see Table 17.1).
plain_en: causes of psychological disorders

name: biomedical model
definition_quote: the biomedical model (or biological perspective) sees psychological disorders as caused by biological factors such as hormonal or neurotransmitter imbalances or by differences in brain structure.
plain_en: disorders caused by biological factors

name: biopsychosocial view
definition_quote: the biopsychosocial view is that problems likely result from the interplay of biological, psychological, and social factors.
plain_en: biological, psychological, and social factors interact

name: diathesis-stress model
definition_quote: According to this model, environmental stressors can provide circumstances under which a biological predisposition for illness can express itself.
plain_en: stress triggers inherited vulnerability to illness

name: eclectic
definition_quote: Psychologists who do not subscribe strictly to one perspective or another are known as eclectic.
plain_en: using several theoretical perspectives together

name: autism spectrum disorder
definition_quote: Children with autism spectrum disorder seek out less social and emotional contact than do other children and are less likely to seek out parental support when distressed.
plain_en: reduced social and emotional contact with others

name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
definition_quote: A child with ADHD may have difficulty paying attention or sitting still.
plain_en: difficulty paying attention or sitting still

name: neurocognitive disorders
definition_quote: The DSM-5 also discusses neurocognitive disorders, the most well-known of which may be Alzheimer’s disease.
plain_en: cognitive decline disorders like Alzheimer's disease

name: Alzheimer’s disease
definition_quote: Alzheimer’s is a form of dementia, a deterioration of cognitive abilities, often seen most dramatically in memory.
plain_en: dementia with deteriorating memory and cognition

name: Anxiety disorders
definition_quote: Anxiety disorders, as their name suggests, share a common symptom of anxiety.
plain_en: disorders sharing anxiety as their common symptom

name: specific phobia
definition_quote: A simple or specific phobia is an intense unwarranted fear of a situation or an object such as claustrophobia (fear of enclosed spaces) or arachnophobia (fear of spiders).
plain_en: intense unwarranted fear of a specific object

name: agoraphobia
definition_quote: Agoraphobia is a fear of open, public spaces.
plain_en: fear of open or public spaces

name: social anxiety disorder
definition_quote: Social anxiety disorder, formerly known as social phobia, is a fear of a situation in which one could embarrass oneself in public, such as when eating in a restaurant or giving a lecture.
plain_en: fear of embarrassing oneself in public

name: taijin kyofusho
definition_quote: It is a type of social anxiety that involves concern that one’s body is displeasing to others.
plain_en: Japanese social anxiety about one's body displeasing others

name: generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)
definition_quote: A person who suffers from generalized anxiety disorder, often referred to as GAD, experiences constant, low-level anxiety.
plain_en: constant low-level anxiety

name: panic disorder
definition_quote: On the other hand, someone with panic disorder suffers from acute episodes of intense anxiety without any apparent provocation.
plain_en: acute intense anxiety without apparent provocation

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Anxiety Disorders
name: Psychodynamic theorists on anxiety disorders
definition_quote: Psychodynamic theorists see psychological disorders as caused by unresolved, unconscious conflicts.
plain_en: unresolved unconscious conflicts cause anxiety disorders

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Anxiety Disorders
name: Behaviorists on anxiety disorders
definition_quote: Behaviorists believe all behaviors are learned. Therefore, they assert that anxiety disorders are learned.
plain_en: anxiety disorders are learned behaviors

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Anxiety Disorders
name: Cognitive theorists
definition_quote: Cognitive theorists believe that disorders result from dysfunctional ways of thinking.
plain_en: disorders come from dysfunctional thinking patterns

name: Somatic symptom disorders
definition_quote: Somatic symptom disorders occur when a person manifests a psychological problem through a physiological symptom.
plain_en: psychological problems expressed through physical symptoms

name: conversion disorder
definition_quote: People who have conversion disorder report the existence of a severe physical problem such as paralysis or blindness, and they will, in fact, be unable to move their arms or see.
plain_en: loss of physical function without physical cause

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Somatic Symptom Disorders
name: Psychodynamic theorists on somatic symptom disorders
definition_quote: Psychodynamic theorists would assert that somatic symptom disorders are merely outward manifestations of unresolved unconscious conflicts.
plain_en: unconscious conflicts expressed as physical symptoms

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Somatic Symptom Disorders
name: Behaviorists on somatic symptom disorders
definition_quote: Behaviorists would say that people with somatic symptom disorders are being reinforced for their behavior.
plain_en: physical symptoms are reinforced behaviors

name: Dissociative disorders
definition_quote: Dissociative disorders involve a disruption in conscious processes; dissociation involves a break or separation from memories and thoughts or even a sense of who the person is.
plain_en: disruption in consciousness, memory, or identity

name: Dissociative amnesia
definition_quote: Dissociative amnesia is when a person cannot remember things and no physiological basis for the disruption in memory can be identified.
plain_en: memory loss without physiological cause

name: organic amnesia
definition_quote: Biologically induced amnesia is called organic amnesia.
plain_en: amnesia caused by biological factors

name: Dissociative identity disorder (DID)
definition_quote: Dissociative identity disorder, formerly known as multiple personality disorder, is when a person has several personalities rather than one integrated personality.
plain_en: several personalities instead of one integrated identity

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Dissociative Disorders
name: Psychodynamic theorists on dissociative disorders
definition_quote: Psychodynamic theorists believe that dissociative disorders result when an extremely traumatic event has been so thoroughly repressed that a split in consciousness results.
plain_en: repressed trauma splits consciousness

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Dissociative Disorders
name: Behaviorists on dissociative disorders
definition_quote: Behaviorists posit that people who have experienced trauma simply find not thinking about it to be rewarding, thus producing amnesia or, in extreme cases, DID.
plain_en: not thinking about trauma is rewarded

name: mood or affective disorder
definition_quote: Someone with a mood or affective disorder experiences extreme or inappropriate emotions.
plain_en: extreme or inappropriate emotions

name: Major depressive disorder
definition_quote: Major depressive disorder, also known as unipolar depression, is the most common mood disorder and is often referred to as the common cold of all psychological disorders.
plain_en: most common mood disorder, unipolar depression

name: Persistent depressive disorder
definition_quote: Persistent depressive disorder is diagnosed when the depression is long-lasting but not as severe.
plain_en: long-lasting but less severe depression

name: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD)
definition_quote: Finally, some people experience depression but only during certain times of the year, usually winter when there is less sunlight.
plain_en: depression tied to seasonal sunlight changes

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Depressive Disorders
name: Psychodynamic theorists on depressive disorders
definition_quote: Psychodynamic theorists may view depression as the product of anger directed inward or an overly punitive superego.
plain_en: anger turned inward or harsh superego

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Depressive Disorders
name: Learning theorists
definition_quote: Learning theorists view the mood disorder as bringing about some kind of reinforcement such as attention or sympathy.
plain_en: depression reinforced by attention and sympathy

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Depressive Disorders
name: cognitive triad
definition_quote: Aaron Beck, a cognitive theorist, believed that depression results from unreasonably negative ideas that people have about themselves, their world, and their futures. Beck calls these three components the cognitive triad.
plain_en: unreasonably negative ideas about self, world, future

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Depressive Disorders
name: attribution
definition_quote: An attribution is an explanation of cause.
plain_en: explanation of a cause

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Depressive Disorders
name: internal, global, and stable attributions
definition_quote: People who tend to make internal, global, and stable attributions for bad events are more likely to be depressed.
plain_en: attributing bad events to internal, global, stable causes

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Depressive Disorders
name: learned helplessness
definition_quote: Learned helplessness is when one’s prior experiences have caused that person to view himself or herself as unable to control aspects of the future that are controllable.
plain_en: believing one cannot control future outcomes

name: bipolar disorder
definition_quote: Unlike unipolar depression, bipolar disorder, formerly known as manic depression, usually involves both depressed and manic episodes.
plain_en: alternating depressive and manic episodes

name: manic episodes
definition_quote: People experience manic episodes in different ways, but they usually involve feelings of high energy.
plain_en: periods of unusually high energy

name: hypomania
definition_quote: The major difference is that bipolar II involves at least one episode of hypomania, which is a less extreme level of mania than in bipolar I.
plain_en: less extreme form of mania

name: schizophrenia
definition_quote: The fundamental symptom of schizophrenia is disordered, distorted thinking often demonstrated through delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking, disorganized speech, and/or disorganized motor behavior.
plain_en: disordered thinking with delusions and hallucinations

name: delusions
definition_quote: Delusions are beliefs that have no basis in reality.
plain_en: beliefs with no basis in reality

name: hallucinations
definition_quote: Hallucinations are perceptions in the absence of any sensory stimulation.
plain_en: perceptions without sensory stimulation

name: neologisms
definition_quote: They may make up their own words (neologisms) or string together a series of nonsense words that rhyme (clang associations).
plain_en: invented meaningless words

name: word salad
definition_quote: As a result, it may be difficult to understand what they are trying to communicate, and the resultant speech has been described as word salad.
plain_en: disorganized speech difficult to understand

name: flat affect
definition_quote: Alternatively, they may consistently have essentially no emotional response at all (flat affect).
plain_en: almost no emotional response

name: catatonia
definition_quote: Some schizophrenics suffer from catatonia, a motor problem.
plain_en: abnormal motor behavior

name: positive symptoms
definition_quote: Positive symptoms refer to excesses in behavior, thought, or mood such as neologisms and hallucinations
plain_en: excesses in behavior, thought, or mood

name: negative symptoms
definition_quote: negative symptoms correspond to deficits such as flat affect or catatonic stupor
plain_en: deficits in normal functioning

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Schizophrenic Disorders
name: dopamine hypothesis
definition_quote: The basic idea behind the dopamine hypothesis is that high levels of dopamine seem to be associated with schizophrenia.
plain_en: high dopamine levels associated with schizophrenia

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Schizophrenic Disorders
name: tardive dyskinesia
definition_quote: However, extensive use of these drugs may also cause negative side effects such as muscle tremors and stiffness, a problem known as tardive dyskinesia.
plain_en: muscle tremors from prolonged antipsychotic drug use

subheading: Theories About the Cause of Schizophrenic Disorders
name: double bind
definition_quote: A double bind is when a person is given contradictory messages.
plain_en: receiving contradictory messages

name: Personality disorders
definition_quote: Personality disorders are well-established, maladaptive ways of behaving that negatively affect people’s ability to function.
plain_en: enduring maladaptive behavior patterns impairing functioning

name: Cluster A
definition_quote: Cluster A is associated with suspicious or eccentric behaviors and includes paranoid, schizoid, and schizotypal personality disorders.
plain_en: suspicious or eccentric personality disorders

name: Cluster B
definition_quote: Cluster B is marked by impulsive or emotional, dramatic, and erratic tendencies and includes antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic, and borderline personality disorders.
plain_en: impulsive, dramatic, erratic personality disorders

name: antisocial personality disorder
definition_quote: People with antisocial personality disorder have little regard for other people’s feelings.
plain_en: little regard for others' feelings

name: borderline personality disorder
definition_quote: Borderline personality disorder can result in unstable social relationships; people who suffer from it can fear abandonment and switch back and forth between how they feel about and act toward others.
plain_en: unstable relationships and shifting emotions

name: narcissistic personality disorder
definition_quote: Narcissistic personality disorder involves seeing oneself as the center of the universe (narcissism means “self-love”), and histrionic personality disorder connotes overly dramatic behavior (histrionics).
plain_en: seeing oneself as center of universe

name: Cluster C
definition_quote: Anxiety is the hallmark of Cluster C, which includes avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders.
plain_en: personality disorders marked by anxiety

name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
definition_quote: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is when persistent, unwanted thoughts (obsessions) cause someone to feel the need (compulsion) to engage in a particular action.
plain_en: persistent unwanted thoughts drive compulsive actions

name: body dysmorphic disorder
definition_quote: However, the DSM-5 has created a separate classification for OCD and related disorders, including hoarding disorder and body dysmorphic disorder (an obsession with perceived defects related to one’s appearance).
plain_en: obsession with perceived appearance defects

name: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
definition_quote: PTSD usually involves flashbacks or nightmares following a person’s involvement in or observation of an extremely troubling event such as a war or natural disaster.
plain_en: flashbacks or nightmares after trauma

name: Paraphilias
definition_quote: Paraphilias, or psychosexual disorders, are marked by the sexual attraction to an object, a person, or an activity not usually seen as sexual.
plain_en: attraction to objects, people, or activities not usually sexual

name: pedophilia
definition_quote: For instance, attraction to children is called pedophilia, to animals is called zoophilia, and to objects, such as shoes, is called fetishism.
plain_en: sexual attraction to children

name: anorexia nervosa
definition_quote: The basic symptoms that result in a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa are being at significantly low weight for one’s age and size, an intense fear of fat and food, and a distorted body image.
plain_en: low weight, fear of fat, distorted body image

name: bulimia
definition_quote: Bulimia commonly involves a binge-purge cycle in which sufferers eat large quantities of food and then attempt to purge the food from their bodies by throwing up or using laxatives.
plain_en: binge eating followed by purging

name: binge-eating disorder
definition_quote: Binge-eating disorder is thought to be the most commonly occurring eating disorder in the United States. It involves eating very large quantities of food in a short time while experiencing feelings of loss of control.
plain_en: large amounts of food, loss of control

name: Substance-related and addictive disorders
definition_quote: Substance-related and addictive disorders is a diagnosis made when the use of such substances or behaviors, like gambling, regularly negatively affects a person’s life.
plain_en: substance use regularly harms one's life

name: diagnostic labels
definition_quote: However, keep in mind that diagnostic labels are not always correct and tend to outlast their usefulness.
plain_en: labels may be inaccurate and outlast usefulness

section: The Advantages and Disadvantages of Diagnostic Labels
name: The Rosenhan study
definition_quote: In 1978, David Rosenhan conducted a study in which he and several associates sought admission to a number of mental hospitals.
plain_en: fake patients admitted to mental hospitals

name: methods of treatment
definition_quote: All the methods of treatment, however, share a common purpose: to alter the client’s behavior, thoughts, and/or feelings.
plain_en: treatment aims to change behavior, thoughts, feelings

name: Psychotherapies
definition_quote: Psychotherapies, except for behavioral treatments, largely consist of talking to a psychologist.
plain_en: therapy mainly through talking with a psychologist

name: Psychoanalysis
definition_quote: Psychoanalysis is a therapeutic technique developed by Sigmund Freud.
plain_en: Freud's therapeutic technique

name: Psychodynamic therapy
definition_quote: Psychodynamic therapy grew out of Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytic approach.
plain_en: therapy derived from Freud's psychoanalysis

name: Symptom substitution
definition_quote: Symptom substitution is when, after a person has been successfully treated for one psychological disorder, that person begins to experience a new psychological problem.
plain_en: new problem appears after successful treatment

name: Free association
definition_quote: More commonly, psychodynamic theorists might ask patients to free associate—to say whatever comes to mind without thinking.
plain_en: saying whatever comes to mind uncensored

name: Manifest content
definition_quote: In dream analysis, what the patient reports is called the manifest content of the dream.
plain_en: dream's surface content as reported

name: Latent content
definition_quote: What is really of interest to the analyst is the latent or hidden content.
plain_en: hidden meaning of a dream

name: Resistance
definition_quote: Since analysis can be a painful process of coming to terms with deeply repressed, troubling thoughts, people are thought to try to protect themselves through resistance.
plain_en: avoiding painful repressed thoughts during therapy

name: Transference
definition_quote: Transference is when, during therapy, patients begin to have strong feelings toward their therapists.
plain_en: strong feelings toward the therapist

name: Insight therapies
definition_quote: Insight therapies highlight the importance of the patients/clients gaining an understanding of their problems.
plain_en: therapies emphasizing insight into one's problems

name: Humanistic therapies
definition_quote: Humanistic therapies focus on helping people to understand and accept themselves and strive to self-actualize.
plain_en: helping clients accept themselves and self-actualize

name: Self-actualization
definition_quote: Self-actualization means to reach one’s highest potential.
plain_en: reaching one's highest potential

name: Determinism
definition_quote: It holds that people have no influence over what happens to them and that their choices are predetermined by forces outside of their control.
plain_en: choices predetermined by forces outside one's control

name: Person-centered therapy
definition_quote: This therapeutic method hinges on the therapist providing the client with what Rogers termed unconditional positive regard.
plain_en: Rogers therapy centered on unconditional positive regard

name: Unconditional positive regard
definition_quote: Unconditional positive regard is blanket acceptance and support of a person regardless of what the person says or does.
plain_en: total acceptance regardless of what client does

name: Active listening
definition_quote: They encourage the clients to talk a lot about how they feel and sometimes mirror back those feelings to help clarify the feelings for the client.
plain_en: listening and mirroring back client's feelings

name: Gestalt therapy
definition_quote: Another type of humanistic therapy is Gestalt therapy, developed by Fritz Perls.
plain_en: Perls's therapy emphasizing whole self and present

name: Existential therapies
definition_quote: Existential therapies are humanistic therapies that focus on helping clients achieve a subjectively meaningful perception of their lives.
plain_en: helping clients find meaning in life

name: Applied behavior analysis (ABA)
definition_quote: One behavioral approach, most used to help people with developmental disorders like autism spectrum disorder, is known as applied behavior analysis (ABA).
plain_en: using reinforcement to shape behavior

name: Counterconditioning
definition_quote: One technique is counterconditioning, a kind of classical conditioning in which an unpleasant conditioned response is replaced with a pleasant one.
plain_en: replacing unpleasant conditioned response with pleasant one

name: Systematic desensitization
definition_quote: This process involves teaching the client to replace the feelings of anxiety with relaxation.
plain_en: gradually replacing anxiety with relaxation

name: Anxiety hierarchy
definition_quote: An anxiety hierarchy is a rank-ordered list of what the client fears, starting with the least frightening and ending with the most frightening.
plain_en: ranked list of fears, least to most frightening

name: Flooding
definition_quote: Unlike the gradual process of systematic desensitization, flooding involves having the client address the most frightening scenario first.
plain_en: confronting the most frightening situation first

name: Modeling
definition_quote: Modeling, as you will recall from Unit 3, is a process through which one person learns by observing and then imitating the behavior of another.
plain_en: learning by observing and imitating others

name: Exposure therapies
definition_quote: However, discussing it with systematic desensitization and flooding makes sense because all three are exposure therapies; all involve some degree of contact with the feared stimuli.
plain_en: therapy involving contact with feared stimuli

name: Aversive therapy
definition_quote: This process involves pairing a habit a person wishes to break, such as smoking or bed- wetting, with an unpleasant stimulus such as electric shock or nausea.
plain_en: pairing bad habit with unpleasant stimulus

name: Token economy
definition_quote: In a token economy, desired behaviors are identified and rewarded with tokens.
plain_en: rewarding desired behaviors with tokens

name: Cognitive therapy
definition_quote: As cognitive therapists locate the cause of psychological problems in the way people think, their methods of therapy concentrate on changing these unhealthy thought patterns.
plain_en: changing unhealthy thought patterns

name: Cognitive restructuring
definition_quote: The goal of cognitive therapy is often referred to as cognitive restructuring, which involves challenging people’s patterns of maladaptive thinking.
plain_en: challenging maladaptive thinking patterns

name: Cognitive triad
definition_quote: Beck explains depression using the cognitive triad: people’s beliefs about themselves, their worlds, and their futures.
plain_en: negative beliefs about self, world, future

name: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
definition_quote: One popular group of therapies combines the ideas and techniques of both cognitive and behavioral psychologists. This approach to therapy is known as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).
plain_en: combines cognitive and behavioral therapy techniques

name: Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT)
definition_quote: Therapists employing REBT look to expose and confront the dysfunctional thoughts of their clients.
plain_en: exposing and confronting clients' dysfunctional thoughts

name: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT)
definition_quote: DBT focuses more on emotions than thought patterns and is often used to help people who have extreme emotional reactions interact with others and their environments in healthier ways.
plain_en: cognitive behavioral therapy emphasizing emotion regulation

name: Group therapy
definition_quote: Sometimes group therapy involves meeting with several people experiencing similar difficulties.
plain_en: multiple people receive therapy together

name: Family therapy
definition_quote: Since a client’s problems do not occur in a vacuum, many therapists find meeting with the whole family helpful in revealing the patterns of interaction among family members and altering the behavior of the whole family rather than just one member.
plain_en: treating the whole family together

name: Self-help groups
definition_quote: Self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) are a form of group therapy that does not involve a therapist at all.
plain_en: group therapy without a therapist

name: Somatic therapies
definition_quote: Therefore, these psychologists advocate the use of somatic therapies—therapies that produce bodily changes.
plain_en: therapies that produce bodily changes

name: Drug therapy or psychopharmacology
definition_quote: The most common type of somatic therapy is drug therapy or psychopharmacology, also known as chemotherapy (see Table 18.2).
plain_en: using medication to treat psychological disorders

name: Antipsychotic medications
definition_quote: Schizophrenia is generally treated with antipsychotic medications such as Thorazine or Haldol. These drugs generally function by blocking the receptor sites for dopamine.
plain_en: block dopamine receptors to treat schizophrenia

name: Tardive dyskinesia
definition_quote: An unfortunate side effect of antipsychotic medication is tardive dyskinesia—Parkinsonian-like, chronic muscle tremors.
plain_en: chronic muscle tremors from antipsychotic medication

name: serotonin selective reuptake inhibitor drugs (SSRIs)
definition_quote: The three most common kinds of drugs used to treat unipolar depression are tricyclic antidepressants, monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors, and serotonin selective reuptake inhibitor drugs or SSRIs (most notably Prozac).
plain_en: antidepressants that increase serotonin activity

name: Lithium
definition_quote: Lithium, a metal, is often used to treat the manic phase of bipolar disorder.
plain_en: metal drug treating manic episodes

name: Biofeedback
definition_quote: During biofeedback, a patient is taught to recognize and then control various physiological responses such as breathing, heart rate, or even brain activity (neurofeedback) without medication.
plain_en: learning to control physiological responses

name: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
definition_quote: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) employs magnets to alter brain activity and is mainly used in the treatment of depression.
plain_en: magnets alter brain activity to treat depression

name: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
definition_quote: Another approach targeted at changing brain activity is electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).
plain_en: electrical current inducing a brief seizure

name: Psychosurgery
definition_quote: Psychosurgery involves the purposeful destruction of part of the brain to alter a person’s behavior.
plain_en: destroying brain tissue to change behavior

name: Prefrontal lobotomy
definition_quote: This operation involved cutting the main neurons leading to the frontal lobe of the brain.
plain_en: cutting neurons leading to the frontal lobe

name: Eclectic therapy
definition_quote: Many therapists do not exclusively use one type of therapy.
plain_en: combining multiple therapy approaches

name: Somatic cognitive therapy
definition_quote: Somatic cognitive therapy is another very common combination eclectic therapy.
plain_en: medication combined with cognitive talk therapy

name: Psychiatrists
definition_quote: Psychiatrists are medical doctors and are therefore the only therapists permitted to prescribe medication in most U.S. states.
plain_en: medical doctors who can prescribe medication

name: Clinical psychologists
definition_quote: Clinical psychologists earn doctoral degrees (PhDs) that require four or more years of study.
plain_en: psychologists holding doctoral degrees

name: Counseling therapists
definition_quote: Counseling therapists or counseling psychotherapists typically have some kind of graduate degree in psychology.
plain_en: therapists with graduate degrees treating milder problems

name: therapeutic alliance
definition_quote: The success of the treatment process is also clearly affected by the relationship between client and therapist—the therapeutic alliance.
plain_en: client-therapist relationship affecting treatment success

name: Evidence-based interventions
definition_quote: Evidence-based interventions have been demonstrated to work through research, but even these approaches will not be effective for everyone all the time.
plain_en: interventions proven effective through research
